div.p: NOTES ON AGRICULTURE HORTI- CULTURE, &e.

Winter oats are being cut on South Lea Farm, at Datchet, and with a continuance of the present splendid weather har- vest operations will soon become pretty general in the home counties of Middlesex, Berke, Bucks, and Surrey. All the cereals are looking well, but the root crops sadly require

rain. The Orkney Ii , uds appear to be a good egg-producing district, as from trustworthy statistics it has been ascertained that during the last 12 months more than 11,000,000 have been sent by steamers and sailing vessels to southern markets. From the various ports in the county 7,023 boxes of eggs were exported. These boxes contained from 120 to IV dozen each, and taking the average at 140 dozen, this gives 983,220 dozen, or 11,798,640 eggs; a fair estimate of this enormous number is got by an average of Bd. per dozen, which is rather under than over the real value here. This gives a total value of £32,774, more than half the free rental of the county, and equal to 20s. per head of the entire

population. °revamp AGRICULTURAL COLLEGE.—Not the least notice- able sentence in the American report of Messrs. Read and Pell, was the emphatic testimony of these gentlemen to the fact, that throughout the wide territory of our great Trans- atlantic competitors there was, at all events, none of that hardly-stirred apathy towards agricultural education which we meet with in this country. "A good agricultural educa- tion, both scientific and practical," was, we were told, every- where within reach of the young farmer of Canada or the United States. Special mention is twice made by the Assistant Commissioners of the facilities enjoyed by colo- nial agriculturists in the well-known Ontario Agricultural College, at Guelph. It is described as a sort of Cirencester, save that, instead of paying large fees, the pupils are at almost a nominal cost boarded, lodged, and instructed, and are paid for their labour. Considerable interest attaches, therefore, to the Sixth Annual Report of College and Ex- perimental Farm at a moment when the old country is beginning to think of following somewhat more fully her colonial daughter's practice. The report in question for 1880. published at Toronto by order of the Legislative Council, is uow before us, and contains a vast mass of highly interesting reading; and we cannot do better than reoommend its perusal by all who are pondering the ques- tion, How can we unite in a feasible manner the scientific and practical training of farmers' sons? Alike in the details of the work done, the numerous experiments faithfully and fully recorded, and the conditions and rules of the college, there is much to be learned from this very fall and sugges- tive report.—Farmers' Chronicle. ORIGIN OF THE MERINO SHEEP.—As the ancient Greeks had no cotton nor silk and very little linen, and as sheep's wool was the principal texture from which their clothes were made they took peculiar care to cultivate with especial care such breeds of sheep as produced very fine wool. Such breeds were those of the Greek city of Tartenum, situated on the Tarentine gulf. In order to improve the fine quality of the wool still more, the sheep were covered with clothes , in cold weather, and it was found by experience that ex- posure to cold made the wool coarser. Thus clothing these sheep from generation to generation resulted in a very deli- cate breed with exceedingly fine wool, according to the law established by Darwin in regard to selection and adaptation to exterior conditions. This product of Greek industry , was transmitted by them to the Romans, whose great agri- cultural author, Colanella, states that his uncle in Spain crossed the fine Tarentine sheep with rams imported from I Africa, and obtained a stronger breed, combining the white- I ness of the fleece of the father with the fineness of the fleece of the mother, and having obtained such results the race was perpetuated. The absence of other fine textures made these Spanish sheep so valuable that in the beginning Of our era they were sold in Rome for 1,000 dols. in gold a I head, an enormous price for those times, when money had much more value than now. When the barbarians invaded Italy these sheep were all exterminated, while the greater portion of the Roman possessions were laid waste. Bat in the less accessible mountains of Spain the Moors preserved the breed, and it is to them that modern Spain owes the merino sheep, which are the direct descendants of this cross breed of the Greek and African ancestors referred to. It is a valuable inheritance, too, which the country owes to the combined Greek, Roman, and Moorish civilisation, and of which our California wool-growers also earn the advantages, by the prosperity of this breed of sheep, which was there a few years ago.--Scientific American. FARMING IN THE NETHERLANDS.—Amongst the recently- published reports of the Assistant-Commissioners to the Royal Commission on Agriculture, there are none more full of information and interest than those of Mr. H. M. Jenkins on the agriculture of the Netherlands and Belgium. In the Netherlands!the depression in agriculture, Mr. Jenkins thinks, is as severe as it is in Great Britain, the price of land hav- ing fallen from twenty to forty and even fifty per cent., in spite of peasant-proprietorship and the system of Tenant. Right which prevails in parts of the country. Indeed, Mr. Jenkins appears to think that these systems have not in any respect moderated the severity of the crisis. Considering the enormous prices lately given for land when it is sold, and the high rent when it is let, with other disadvantages, it is no cause for wonder if such is the case. Although there are many small proprietors, the prevailing system is a miniature of the English one of landlord, tenant, and labourer; and under it, Mr. Jenkins say s, "probably most readers of this report will come to the conclusion that the landlord generally obtains more than his fair share of the pro- duce of the soil, and the labourer much less than we should consider him entitled to, while the farmer is even more hampered than in England with written restrictions as to cropping and sale of produce, and does not even understand the phrase 'compensation for unexhausted improvements.'" Thaprice of land varies from £3O to £134 per acre, while rentievstk from ss. 4d. to £l3 13s. 4c1., the high price being given for tobacco land. From £3 to £4 an acre seems to be quite a common rent for arable land. No wonder the farmers of Holland feel the depression. Farms are usually let on leases of seven years, and occasionally for longer periods. The conditions vary in different provinces, but, generally, the mode of farming is more or less prescribed. Manure and straw must usually be consumed on the holding, and the cropping provisions are frequently very minute and stringent. Farms are let by tender very generally in Fries- land, and sometimes in other provinces. A certain amount of fixity of tenure is recognised when there is no written law, as the Code Civil enacts that a farm so taken may be held a sufficient time to enable the farmer to carry out the course of cropping current in the district. Thus,. in Zee- land, a farm held on an unwritten lease would be' tra for seven years. The code also secures to the tenant, in the absence of a special agreement, a right to be reimbursed for loss of crops caused by bad seasons, hail, or tire; but this is usually set aside by contract. The disadvantages of the restrictions of cropping and sale of produce are clearly shown in the report. The Law of Distress prevails in Hol- land, as in other countries where the Code Napoleon is the law of the land. The owner may seize all the property of the tenant for payment of three years' rent besides that of the current year; but prior to his claim are those for seed, labour, and otber expenses of the growing crop. At the present time, the report states, many tenants owe two or even three years' rent. With regard to improvements, Mr. Jenkins says :—" The leases contain no stipulation, except that they must not be executed without the consent of the proprietor; and in that case the payment to the farmer in respect of them is agreed upon. But generally the landlord undertakes such works, pays for them, and charges the tenant an additional rent." If, as Mr. Jenkins 'says, the tenants in the Netherlands do not understand the phrase "compensation for unexhausted improvements," they .are familiar with something a great deal better. In Groningen the system of tenure known as the Beklemregt prevails. It I may be defined as a system of perpetual leases at fixed rents,' with fines to the lord of the manor on changes of tenancy.' The " Beklemde Meiger" (tenant) may sell his Beklemming as a whole, raise money on it, or devise it subject to the law of the land; but he cannot divide it. The system closely resembles that recently referred to by us as existing in the Miniso, the most prosperous province of Portugal, so well described by Mr. Oswald Cranford, H.M. Consul at Oporto, 414111 s interesting book "Portugal Old and New." MO. ",gfte.NeTthheerlßanedecokidamie,timae ,paveleye wrote favourably of the Beklemregt in his book on withamitgihstnneedotalmunedchinlikGeNit,nbile pity England t hat andt h the Scotland GovernmentW did not Andy this system and the similarly emphytentic system of Northern Portugal before they framed the 'risk Land Bill.—Mark Lane Express. Yotmo CHICKENS DESTROYING Irzszers.—The practice Of excluding young chickens from the garden especially in nraedmg Ireland,tti amiss. mid-summer, is bad both for the chickens and for the vege- tables. The young chicks will not thrive in confinement as In freedom, and the growing plants are in good measure protected from insects' by the chickens: -We have never succeeded better with young broods than by putting them with the mother in the vegetable garden. The mother is contliseclie a coop, and the chickens have free access to her through the slats. She follows her instinct in scratching over the ground under the coop for worms and grubs, and after a few days the coop is pushed along to new soil. The chickens somethingalsntt system ms inais highly very v are regularly fed with scalded meal or boiled screenings. They supply themselves with animal food from the garden. The chickens are too small to do any; harm to plants that are well started, and yet they pick up an immense number of insects. The more highly the garden is manured the more rapidly do insects multiply, and the greater is the need of birds and fowls to keep them in check. The chickens can go beneath cucumbers, squashes, beans, tomatoes, Sm., and pick the eggs and worms from the underside of the leaves, found. They eagerly chase leaves, where they are gene every moth and bug that flies, and if one alights within When the striking distance it is sure to be devoured. chickens are large enough to do injury to the plants theyi are easily removed to other quarters.—New d York Her. THE RATABLE VALVE OF RAILWAYS.--AS all illustration of what may be done towards levelling up railway assess- ment, it may not be inappropriate to quote the relief which has just been secured without any formal local taxation re- form by the ratepayers of the Droitwich Union. Under the valuations recently effected by Messrs. Hedley, Mason, and Hadley, the assessment of the railways and their stations in the eighteen townships of this union has been raised more than 100 per cent., or from a ratable value of £14,529 to £33,475, an addition this of no less than £18,946 to the assessable area of the union. This is of course a virtual gain of so much new property brought in to bear the local charges of the union, and pro tanta to lighten the burden of the rural ratepayers. The mere statement of a total increase is of course evidence of the glaring under-assessment of this particular sort of property at this time. The extent to which this under-valuation has been in many instances too long permitted to remain unchallenged, is still more readily apparent if we examine the case of the separate townships of this Droitwich Union. SONG TO A SAILOR. The wind-ho, the wind-ho. It speeds from out the west Like thrushes after even song Towards the mossy neat; With flying feet and piping hands It moves amid the trees, And ...ems to bring the voice to me Of far-Mt restless seas. The wind-ho, the wind-ho. I list to it and dream Of foam-crests white as sea-gull wings Athwart the sunlight's gleam; I hear the gentle, tapping touch Of wavelets 'gainst the quays, And see our blue eyed sailor lad

- - Upon the open seas. The wind-ho, the wind-ho, Phys o'er his white-winged ship, It puts a smile upon his face, And kisses on his lip; It Wks to him of woodland ways And flowery English leas, And makes his heirt beat bold and free _ .

Upon the foaming seas. The wind-ho, the wind-ho, It sighs and falls asleep, But cannot win my thoughts again From off the murm'rous deep; The thrush may tremble into song, The sunset thrill the trees, But oh to see our sailor lad Safe home across the seas.

Economy is an abused word. Most people think of it as a eating of money, as though to be economical was certain, in a sense, to be stingy or mean. Now, economy, in its true interpretation is the art of management—is the wise adapta- tion by which we arrange time, health, and strength so as to produce the best results. Master Mason, of Trinity College, sent his pqpil to another of the masters to borrow a book of him. The pupil was told, " I am loth to lend my books out of my chamber, but, if it please thy tutor to come and read it here, he shall as long as he will" It was winter, and some days after the same master sent to Mr. Mason to borrow his bellows • but Mr. Mason said, "I am loth to lend my bellows out of my chamber, but if thy tutor would come and use it here, he shill as long a.s he will." Jam Webster was brought before an Austin justice of the peace. It was the same old charge that used to bother him so much in Galveston. After the evidence was all in, the judge, with a perplexed look, said i " But I do not comprehend, Webster, how it was possible for you to steal those chickens when they were roosting right under this owner's window, and there were two vicious dogs in this yard." " Hit wouldn't do yer a bit of good, jedge, for rnle to splain how I cotched dam chickens, for yer couldn't do it yerself if ye tried it forty times, and yer might get yer hide full of buckshot de berry fast time yer put yer leg ober de fence. De bee way for yer to do, jedge, is fer yer to buy yer chickens in de market.”----- ill I "Any chestnuts round here?" asked one of three boys who met an aged, benevolent-looking farmer. The old man hesitated. "You don't want to steal 'em?" he asked. " Gli, no! We just wanted to find out." "Wall, there's a fee trees back there; bat if I thought you wanted to steal thorn I wouldn't have told woo, for the owner has gone to town. But you're bright, honest-looking boys." The boys blushed with the pride of COUSCIOUS goodness. "When will the owner be back?" "Well, not before dark, I reckon." The boys respectf ally thanked the old man, waited till he gdt out of sight, jumped the fence, and were soon shaking down ethe burrs. The shaking was easy; but the opening of the chestnut burrs was more difficult and unpleasant. At i thst boys had a splendid pile of handsome brown nuts on th 11 ground, and they prepared to put them in the bags the "brought with them. "Please don't take any more trouble, said the benevolent old man' who stood by the fence, beaud. log kindly on the startled boys. "I'm not so strong as I once was, and I fear I can't hold in this dog mnch longer. It you'll hurry, though, I guess! can keep him here till you get to the railroad fence. Down, Tige, sir !" As the boys looked back from the railroad fence, they could see the stooping figure of the old man scooping the rich brown chestnuts into a two-bushel bag. - Dryzasrry ov Coln/sm.—Lord Granville gave an amus- ing account of the diversity of counsel which has more than once added to the torment of gout. At Rome he was inundated' with prescriptions not only in English and Italian, but in French and German, and even in Russian. The Cat- dinal Secretary of State was good enough to give him some advice based upon his own experience; a Northern foreign minister gave him exactly the apposite advice. In London, in the same way,on the announcement of an attack helm tosched by receiving weekly, and even daily and kourly, letters of advice of an infinite variety. He ought to drink 'whisky, he ought to drink claret, he ought to adhere to the most rigid teetotalism. He had been advised to live generously, and he had been advised almost to starve himself, and one gentleman advised him to obtain a complete set of artificial back teeth. This is the experiment of all of us, but the same experiment applies to other matters besides health. About marriage about the education of children, about money—the variety of advice is just as distracting as it is about gout. In all of them, and in health especially, it is safe to assume that every preposition which claims to be of universal fitness must be untrue. Any layman can see for himself that half the blunders of the doctors arise from thinking that the same treatment must be good for the same • disorder in every case. That steady moderate exercise is good for everybody, male and female, is almost the one single maxim of universal application in the whole of the daygienics.—Pall Mall Gazette. '' Taw Freak &SKr ON CaTS.—At the New York Cat Show the prize for the cat essay ($10) was awarded to Walter C. thieved°, of Brooklyn, his effort being the best of 557. It WRS as follows :—The cat is a cuss that mews and pars, be- cause purr-haps it a-mews-see him. He is covered with fur, and is filled with deceitfulness, and abounds in cheek. I said that on purr-puss. He can place himself outside of a canary in full bloom and then come and sit by your side and look up into your face with a smile that is childlike and bland, chuck full of penitence and canary. Canary other animal do this? His far is soft and glossy, but what this is fur I cannot say. It isn't so soft, however, but what at will break bricks. The cat is a smaller bird than the mule. As a general thing the cat can draw more than any other animal except a mustard plaster. I have known him to ' draw two bootjack% a scuttle of coal, two or three charges out of a gun, two or three swears out of a man, and Other articles of bedroom furniture out of the third storey win- dow. This' can also be said of the average German band. In fact, they are somewhat related, as the discoverer of the fiddle, listening to the music of the cat, cut him open to see where the music came from, and thus laid the founda- tion for fiddle-strings. Cats and fiddles thus became vile Instigators of suicide. They are unfeeline. I would say something about the cat-o'-nine tails, but it is a painful subject; another reason is, I don't know anything about them. See Mr. Bergh. Please send the ten dollars by any of my kind reportorial friends. You might also send a s aceman with a reporter.—Yours categorically. The Government inquiry respecting the position of the powder magazines in the Mersey was concluded on Wednes- day. Admiral Spratt; the conservator of the Mersey, sug- gested that the vessels should be surrounded with galvanised wire petting; he considered the present the best site for the magazines. Mr. Tobin said the Government allowed them to have in the magazines 5,000 barrels of 100Ibs. each, that being the maximum quantity. The memorial stones of new Wesleyan day and Sunday schools were laid at Blackley, on Saturday afternoon. Some novelty was lent to the proceedings by the presence of the rector of the parish, the Rev. W. Coghlan, who in the course of an address advocated more unity between Churchmen and Dissenters. In being present on such an occasion he believed he was but following the footsteps and example of the Bishop of the diocese and of the late Dean Stanley. He was very glad to unite with the Wealeyans of Blackley on that occasionr and wished success to their , schools. AN EXTRAORDINARY APPLICATION —VICARIOUS IMPRI- SONNENT.—An extraordinary application was made at the Fenton Stipendiary Court, on Friday, when Mr. Welch, eplicitor, asked his werahip, on behalf of a druggist named Wooley—recently fined £5O and coats for selling beer and spirits without a license—to allow another man named Coates to undergo a month's imprisonment instead of the defendant. The stipendiary, solicitor, and all present were exceedingly amused at the application, and treated it as a joke, to the evident chagrin of the defendant, who had waited all day for the decision, and who had arranged to give Coates £2. Mr. Goschen was entertained on Wednesday night at a hanquet of the City Liberal Club. London. Referring to his recent services, he said he was accredited to a Power which was suffering under the calamities of a great war; there were anxieties in Asia and Africa; as well as Europe; the soldiers who had to fight the Puselans were wanted to till the fields; and in addition to war, insurrection, and famine, the Turkish Government had to meet the wants of the sub- jects who left the territory ceded to Rtissia. In every part of that empire anarchy prevailed. One of the pashas had told him that in Asia Minor they had not one but 15 Ire- lands to deal with., „ The half-yearly meeting of the Manchester. Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway Company was held on Wednesday. The Chairman (Sir Edward W. Watkin, Bart., M.P.) ex- Dressed regret that the balance available for dividend this half-year was only £2,431 as against £57,134 a year ago. He attributed the falling off in the receipts of the Company to the exceptionally severe winter, the operation of foreign tariffs, and thl very, unfortunate state of the iron and steel trade. It is a significant fact, mentioned by Sir Edward, that the increased German tariffs have had the effect of reducing the exports of cotton and woollen fabrics from Grimsby to the extent of 50 per cent. James Marler, cotton broker, of Newton Moor, Cheshire, was indicted at the Chester Assizes, en Wednesday, for in- flicting grievous bodily harm on his wife, on the 4th of May last, and also with wounding her with intent to mur- der on the Bth of May. The prisoner married his wife in April last. He asked her to lend him £lOO out of a sum of £5OO which she had in her own right, and when she declined he taunted her with having earned themoney in an immoral manner, after which he attacked her as alleged in the indictment. The prisoner was given into custody, com- mitted for trial, and admitted to bail. Whilst he was on bail they still lived amicably together, and on this fact coming out, his Lordship directed the jury .to return a ' verdict of guilty on the minor count of wounding, and he sentenced the prisoner to a week's imprisonment. FIGHT IN A Ittrantsmtc CHIJACIL—There has been a renewal of the disturbances at St. James's, Hateham. The Ritualists had taken advantage of the absence of Mr. Church- warden Sanders to decorate the church for the festival of St. James, on Monday night. Mr. Sanders, however, who was informed of these proceedings, suddenly returned, had the decorations removed, and, with the assistance of his friends, prevented the preacher from getting into the pulpit. .Being thus prevented from entering the pulpit, the rev. gentleman, Without uttering a word, turned back and walked to the chancel steps, and there preached his sermoa, the point in his sermon being to persevere in what was con- sidered right, notwithstanding difficulties thrown in the way by those who thought otherwise. The service over, groups of persons outside discussed the events of the evening. When Mr. Sanders was passing one of these groups, Mr. Croom, churchwardeu to the Rev. Arthur Tooth during that gentleman's incumbency at Hatcham, uttered the word "Thief." Mr. Sanders no sooner heard it than he sprang towards Mr. Croom and struck him a heavy blow on the side of the head. The group immediately closed upon Mr. Sandere, and a tight, in which a stick and umbrella were freely used, followed, Mr. Sanders striking out vigorously at his assailants, and losing his hat in the encounter.

SCIENTIFIC NOTES. CUTTING A Timm SET OF Tatern.—Professor Owen, in the current number of the "Journal of the British Dental Association," says:—" Teeth are organs that, as a rule, have a term of existence more limited than that of the organism of which they form part. In many of the lower vertebrates they are shed very soon after they are completed and in use and are as quickly replaced by others. In the marn- malia, however, there is but one succession of teeth natur- ally shed; but, though the successors et the so-called milk teeth' last long enough to acquire the title of permanent.' they are rarely retained to a very advanced age. There is, however, a belief entertained by many of the occasional acquisition of a third set in human centenarians. Thus, it Is recorded of the Countess of Desmond, in 'Fynes Mori.on's Itinerary' (1617), that, not many years before her death, which 'is said to have occurred at the age of 140 years, 'she had all her teeth renewed.' I was led into a discussion on this point by a worthy clergyman at the house of a friend whom I was visiting, and to my scepticism as to the alleged age and third set of teeth of the old Countess, he replied that there then lived in his parish an old woman alleged te have passed her hundredth year, who was actually then cutting her third set of teeth. I rejoiced at this instance. I had long been convinced that actual phenomena had sug- gested the statement, but that the nature of these had been misinterpreted, and I deemed myself most fortunate in hav• log an opportunity of testing the matter. The following morning I was driven to the old woman's cabin. It was in the north of Ireland, and she was sitting crouching over her peat fire, a typical example of human decay. To the shouts of her pastor the deaf old crone replied by pulling down her skinny lip and exposing the side of her lower jaw, from which there projected through the gum the blackened stump of a tooth, the crown of which had gone many years before. The absorption of the gums, consequent on the edentulous state of the jaw in senility, had brought to light this rem- nant of a long lost tooth. Other stumps of teeth, of which the loss of the decayed crown had been forgotten, might, in like manner, appear through the shrinkage and absorption of the senile jaw. And this I take to be the true ground of the allegations as to the acquisition in extreme old age of a third set of veritable teeth.' Art is not science, nor is the progress made in the one ever like the progress made in the other.— William Hazlitt. Much as the progress made In recent years by the Japanese towards adapting themselves to Western ideas has directed
attention to that part of the world our knowledge of Japan and its modern inhabitanMis still of the vaguest character.
Information which must be valuable, because authentic, is supplied by a careful and elaborate report recently presented _ . _

to his Government by the United States Consul-General in Japan. This report is published in a Japan daily paper lately sent to us, and a summary of its leading features will probably be found to interest many of our readers who may be glad to know something more about "the Flowery Land" and its people. The population of the Japan Islands is between 35 and . .

36 millions; the males being somewhat in excess of the females. Two millions of the inhabitants belong to what may be called the aristocratic class—the higher and lower nobility. A million and a half are merchants, a million mechanics, and 15 millions more or less associated with

agriculture. As to the climate observations taken I Yokohana for a period of nine years show that the annual mean temperature is 571 Fahr., and the Innual rain fall 71'17 inches; June and September being the heaviest months. 17p to 1868 the Government of Japan was absolute and irresponsible, with an Emperor at its head, who held all authority by Divine Right, and who ruled, through a number of princes at whose head stood the Tycoon. In 1868, the Government was essentially remodelled. The feudal system was abolished. Although the poorer classes have no voice with the making and execution of the laws, they have been materially benefited by the change. A system of courts has been established where they can be heard, against even the higher classes. They can claim the intervention of these courts to insure the payment of wages, which they could not do under the old organisation. A burdensome system of men-at-arms has been set aside, and the old divisions of the people abolished in the eyes of the law. Under the old order all the land of the Empire was the Emperors, through the Tycoon it was granted to military favourites, who in turn leased it to farmers in small divisions. Since 1868 the land has been sold, and is held in fee.simple. About three-tenths of all tilled land are now in the posses- sion of small proportions, the balance being held in larger divisions. Formerly paterfamilias had almost unlimited control over all the members of the family. Much of this power has now been done away with, but his authority is still incomparably greater than in any Western Society. The religion of the great mass of the people is Buddhism, not the Buddhism of Endia, but a system grafted upon the original Pagan worship, and retaining much of the gross superstitions of the latter. The common people everywhere believe in shrine cure, and the result is a large number of diseased persons. The priesthood, although less than formerly, is still a mighty power with the lower classes, and the income of shrines and temples, although materially reduced, is still immense, and a most oppressive burden to the people. The whole system of Education has since 1868 been re- modelled. Public Schools have been established, and scien- tific text books from. Europe and America have been trans- _

lated and brought into use. The scientific learning of the West has largely taken the place of the useless proverbs and superstitions of the East, and it is believed that at the present rate of educational progress another decade will see a useful education within reach of every Japanese labourer. The report of the Minister et Education for the year 1879 shows that there were at that time 25,459 elementary schOols in the Empire, 59,825 teachers, and 2,066,566 scholars, out of a school population of 5,251,000. There I were 389 schools of a higher grade with 20,522 scholars, and 96 normal schools with 7,949 scholars. Public libraries have also been opened. One at Tokeo has 70,000 volumes. Alrthe local governments have opened hospitals, with a foreign surgeon for each and a class of medical students. Under the head of "morals" the Report* points out that the number of unmarried men among the labouring class is very lurge, and these spend much of their earnings ia gambling and dissipation. The strong drink is "sake," a distilled spirit made mostly from rice, and of about the strength of ordinary table sherry. While cheap sea transportation is everywhere available, there is in the inarior a great lack of good roads. There are some 'few hundred miles orrailway, but, practically speaking. from and to tke interior districts all the products and all articles Of trade are Carried on the backs of men or horses. Mails have been eetablished within the last ten years, both coast wise and inland, and postage is cheap and excellent. There are 3,927 post-offices, and the number of letters and newspapers carried for the year ending Jane, 1880, was nearly 67 millions. Although there are un- limited quantities of good durable building stone and vast deposits of firm clay, no stone or brick houses are built. The frequency and severity of earthquakes make the use of any but wooden structures impracticable. All buildings, Or I nearly all, are of one storey, and, compared to those of Europe and America, small. The farmer is now the owner of the soil he tills. Japan farming has no season of rest, as in colder climates; the weather in nearly all parts of the country being so mild in winter as to admit of raising the hardier crops. A consider- able, per 'centage of the farmers are not workers; large num- bers of the tea, silk, rice, tobacco, and sugar raisers being able to employ labourers for that purpose. Almost every farmer can read, write, and keep his farm accounts. He sends his son to some school to learn the same, and has his daugh- ters taught maid° and needlework at home. Every farmer's house has its wheel and loom. All labour on the land is up to the present mere hard work. The area in actual cultivation in the whole empire was, a few years ago, twelve million acres or three-fourths of an acre per head only of the farming population. Rice and wheat are grown in all parts, and the climate and soil are everywhere available for barley. The tea culture is one of the most important and lucrative of all Japanese industries, and the export has wonderfully increased In the export of tea there are employed a large number of carpenters in making boxes, and printers and lithographers in the making of labels, &c., who are paid as skilled labourers. Mulberry plantations are found in fifty of the sixty-six provinces of Japan, and the silk trade is steadily growing and giving increased employment to labour. It is generally believed that the cotton manufac- tures have increased within the past few years from 30 to 50 per cent. The cotton itself is coarse, and in consequence the manufactured cloth is of inferior quality. There is hardly a house in Japan where some mechanical trade is not carried on. Even in the households of the I higher classes, silk, cotton, and other goods are made by the servants, and the members of the family have some know- ledge of the art. As stated above, there is a wheel and loom in every farmhouse, and many of the smaller merchants make more or less of their goods. Thus there are many more artisans in the country than are shown by the census. There are five or six millions who work more or less at mechani- cal trades. Many of the wares used for home consumption .require no special skill in their production, and therefore the labour wage is low. In the manufacture of silk, lacquer, I porcelain, enamels, bronzes, embroideries, and in their paint- ings, skilled labour must enter, and is paid for accordingly. The mechanical, like the agricultural, work is in the main hand labour. Porcelain and earthenware are manufactured in every province, and with one exception, that of the home department in the province of Hizen, there is no foreign machinery or mode of manufacture in use. The clay is manipulated as it was in the earlier days. There is, of course, a numerous fishing population in Japan. Every shore has its fishing villages. The Consul- General is inclined to think that the fishing class if; the lowest in the country. Their houses are the poorest and the dirtiest and they are the least intelligent. As to the sports and pastimes of the Japanese, it may be mentioned that theatrical performances are popular; that under the harvest moon a whole village can be seen collected to wit- DNS wrestling, racing, and fencing. Labouring men in the evening go to tea-honses, drink "sake," play games of skill, and sing songs, while women and girls gossip in groups at some neighbour's house or at the public baths. They also play a game of checkers, while the men are skilled in chess. It follows, from the widespread belief in shrine cures, that the Japanese are great in pilgrimages. Friends and neighbours visit shrines and temples in the mountains one or two hundred miles away from their homes, going on foot all the way, and in the middle of the day, when tired, sleeping in the shade of the groves. Every branch of labour and trade has its guild, zealously guarding the in. terests of its members, and if labour-saving machinery, large capital, and great establishments should ever be intro- duced, these guilds may assume, as with trade organisations here, very great importance. A line, in conclusion, as to the scenery of the country, which has been called the Eng- land of the Pacific. The remarkable scenery of Japan has won the admiration of every visitor. The grand mountain ranges covered with trees and shrubs clothed with per- petual green; the charming and picturesque valleys, car- peted with richest verdure and blossoming with flowers of a thousand hues; the rushing torrents and winding rivers, and the skies of palest blue, all combine to make Japan beautiful in the extreme.

Bo ir SMOKERS.—Whatever- difference there may be amongst members of the medical profession as to the effects of the moderate use of tobacco by adults, the discussion in our columns at the commencement of the year 1880 of the subject of smoking revealed a pretty general agreement in the conclusion that the employment of the rnarcotic weed by persons of immature years was wholly and distinctly detrimental. Some time ago a law was passed in Germany to prohibit the use of tobacco by boys tinder fifteen, either at home or in the streets. Several of the Swiss cantons have now, it is stated, followed the example of their big neighbour, and made it illegal for youths to indulge in the deleterious habit. Half an hour's stroll in the streets of Loudon is Bufficient to engender in the peregrinator a wish that something could be done in this country to check the consumption of tobacco by little boys whose mouths are more fitted to receive a stick of barley-sugar than a short black pipe.—Lancet. 21.0 TO £SO.—TOBACCONISTS 0024MENCING.—A. div.head: PIANOFORTE, ANCIENT AND
div.p: THE PIANOFORTE, ANCIENT AND
MOD ERN, The pianoforte is pre-eminently a modern instrument, yet its origin is already lost in the darkness of ages, or at least in the obscurity of the 17th and leth centuries. Traces

of the piano have even been found in the 16th century; for, in a letter, dated June, 1578, from a musical instrument maker named Paliarino to Alphonoso' second Duke at Modena, the word is at /east mentioned, though musical antiquaries have not yet come to an understanding' aitn what it really meant. It isto be feared that the instrument described by Paliarino as the" piano e forte," with an organ underneath, must have been a species of harmonium; an un- musical contrivance which would thus be entitled to claim such respectability as can be derived from antiquity. A second letter of Paliarine's has been discovered, in which he speaks of the "piano e forte," and goes on to deintrihe it is "the instrument on which the duke plays." 'Then, propos- ing to construct a new one, he requests his correspondent to buy him for that purpose ".lin3e-tree, boxwood, and ebony for keys, cyprus for the belly, brass wire, and German glue." Out of glue, wire, ebony, and wood, what, even in the present day would be considered a very fair piano might be manufactured, though in pianos of the latest make and of the greatest power a considerable quantity of iron is DM used. Heine, in his letters to the Allgemeine Zeitunq on the musical doings of the Parisians, spoke of the pianists with whom the French capital at that time swarmed as "artists in wood." "Artists in iron" would be a &ter expression in the present day; and the increased sonority which the substitution in the internal mechanism of iron for wood has enabled the manufacturer to obtain, has been accompanied by a corresponding augmentation of force, which now and then takes the form of violence on the part of the performer. Writing of the thundering style in which the lion pianists of 35 years ago performed, the afore- said Heim wrote, when, after dismissing others he came to Dryschock, "Surely some faint echo of his playing must, when the wind was blowing towards Germany, have reached the ears of my readers.' Yet connoisseurs who heard Dryschock in 1846, and who listened to the performances of Rubinstein only the other day, declare that the German giant, who so astounded Heinrich Heine, was much inferior in power to the Russian Titan of our own time. Such may be the case. But thelact must be taken into consideration that the pianos of the present day are much more formidable iestruments than were those of more than a quarter of a century ago. A greater volume of sound can be extracted from them, and, without offence to Rubinstein, whose pianissimi are as beautiful as his fortissimi are amazing, the mere production of sound seems now more than ever to be the object of the player. All things taken into account, the piano is, beyond deubt, the most useful and, in many respects, the most beautiful of musical instruments ; and stress should be laid on this fact, because it is the fashion in many quarters to ignore it. As the notes cannot be sustained, it is impossible to obtain on the piano such a Legato as the violinist or the violincel- list produces; and in strict acoustics the notes of the piano are inexact, But, probably, no violinist has ever played 's° precisely, so mathematically in tune, that he could affind to despise the theoretic imperfection of the pianoforte scale; and the groat masters of the instrument, if they eannot rival joachim and Piatti in legato playing, can, at least, execute cantabile passages with marvellous expression, and thus succeed in suggesting what they do not altogether ac- complish. But the great, the incomparable superiority of the piano over all the instruments ordinarily employed in, the orchestra is that it is an orchestra in itself ; so that in the pianoforte version'of the most massive, most elaborate symphony, all the harmonies of the original can be repro- duced. • Asa natural consequence of the utility and beauty of the piano, all the great composers, who have devoted themselves to concert music, have written specially for this instrument,. Lis the only instrument for the composer who may 'wish from time to time hi try the effect of what he has been riling, and it is the second Instrument of every exectdant who does not 'take it his first.

, Although musical doctors differ as to who made the first piano, the honour of having invented the instrument is generally ascribed to the Italian Cristotori ; and not many years ago the centenary of the piano was celebrated with much pomp, and naturally with some noise, in more than one of the great Italian cities: On this occasion the date from which the hundred years of, the piano's existanc.e had been computed was 1776. But the Germans, of course, claimed to, have made pianos long before the year in which Cristofori is held by his fellow-countrymen to have turned out the first comparatively perfect instrument of the piano type. It is certain, moreover, that, in 1767, the piano figured prominently ,in the orchesira at Covent Garden Theatre • for, a playbill of that year announces.(under, date May'lq that "Miss Brickler wilt ainga favourite song from 'Judith: accompanied by Mr. Dibilin on a new instrument called pianoforte:" It was_ not, however, need-as a kilo instrument until a year later, when John Christian Bach performed on it at the "Thatched House." It is recorded too,'that, in 1710, Mr. Burney, nephew of Dr. Harney, the musical historian, was appointed to the pianoforte" at Drury Lane; but no one knows what pianos these were, nor of whose make. Whatever the age of the piano, it may safely be said that pianoforte playing is at this moment scarcely more than 100 years old; for the musicians who took to Cristofori's instrument had fornied their style on the harpsta chord and spinet, which the piano was destined to displace Mozart, for instance, who, as every amateur of music knows; wrote numbers of very melodious sonatas for the pianoforte; was never a piinist in the true sense of the word, because he could never free himself from the touch he had acquired as a player on the harpsichord. Strange instruments the pianos, even the best ones, of Mozart's time, must have been. In 1777, a year after the annus mirabilis, in which the piano is supposed to have been given to a delighteell world by Cristofori, Mozart made the acquaintance at Augs4 burg of a new piano, manufactured by an organ buildet named Stein, and was charmed by its perfection. In a letter to his father he exclaims with a sort of ecstacy that "the action never blocks, and never fails to sound—as is some- times the case with other pianos. On the other hand," he continues, "it never sounds too long, and the machine, pressed by the knee, is prompt to raise the dampers, or, on discontinuing the pressure ever so little, is as prompt to let them down upon the strings." It is easy to claim for the piano such merit as may belong to ancient descent. But, as a matter of fact, it no more dates from the sixteenth, sevenr teenth, or even eighteenth century than do many worthy families which, like the piano, have only recently become known, and which, unlike the piano, are self-made; pianos and pianists came into existence about the same time. As soon, that is to say, as pianos worth playing on were manu- factured, a number of able musicians began to play on them. Among the earliest of these Clementi and Dussek, Cramer, Field, and Hummel may be named; and it is known that Clementi, however artistic his style may have been, was so poor a master of what is called "technique," that, in his latter days, he affected to have lost all taste for pianoforte playine, the fact being that he had never gained that com- mand over the resources of the instrument which his younger competitors had set themselves to acquire. Hew the art of grappling with technical difficalties—difficulties were intro- duced for the sake of being overcome—has marched since then. There has been as great a change in the method of pianoforte playing as in the manufacture of pianofortes; the execution of a Rubinstein surpassing that of Clementl as much as a modern "concert grand" surpasses the feeble in- struments which were in use at the beginning of the century. The investigation of these matters appertaining to ancient and modern pianos of all hinds, induced a desire to request permission to examine the best and mast famous produc- tions of the present day, and fortunately the eminent manu- factory of Messrs. John Brlnamead and Sons at Kentish Town, was selected. The founder of this business, Mr. John Brinsmead, established it in 1836, his staff then con- sisti ig of two men and a boy. The rapid strides and pro- gress since achieved may be imagined when fully 300 hands are now employed, and more than 50 pianos a Week are solo and produced in the highest style of excellence. The firm have orders now on hand which they cannot exe- cute for nearly three months to come, even at this great rate of production which is unsurpassed by any ether manufactory. The great demand has rendered necessary the erection of an additional factory, which will be com- pleted before the end of this month. Mr. John Brinsrnead, who was originally a cabinet maker, and came to London from North Devon, has always taken the greatest interest itt the manufacture of pianos, and it has been the pride of h life to produce the best article possible, and he is constant) introducing improvements. Although 45 years' hard wor and practical knowledge have produced such prospero results, Mr. Brinsmead takes as much interest as ever every detail, the most important finishing process "touch," "voicing," &c., being his special province, and in which his experience and knowledge is unrivalled Messrs. Brinamead have patented at different times t perfect check-repeater action, and also the sostenenie sounding board, capable of sustaining sound for 60 seconda, the great charm of the piano being very much enharsce!l hereby. Every portion of a piano is ready to hand at these works, and a complete piano in all its details could be put together on one floor in an incredibly short space of time. At the least, 300 or 400 pianos are in course of manufacture, and the minutest detail is personally looked after by the princi- pal. The number of gold medals gained by the firm at all principal exhibitions is very numerous, and at the three recent ones in Queensland, Sydney, and Melbourne. the first prize for uprights and grands has been awarded to them. The present manufactory was built about ten years ago upon plans by Mr. Brinsmead himself, and is most complete in every sense. No expense has been spared where neces- sary, and nothing has been expended that could be avoided. To any one desirous of extending his knowledge of pianos, their manufacture at the present day, with all the improve ments of science and the experience carefully gained during Son's a lifetime, a visit to Messrs. John Brinsrnead and manufactory, under the guidance of the founder, will afford a pleasure they cannot appreciate until experienced. PartBRTUAL PENSIONS.—Lord ROSEBERY presented a peti- tion from the Convention of Royal and Parliamentary Bearghs of Scotland, praying for an inquiry into the perpe- tual pensions now made by the Treasury. THE PATRIOTIO Foam—The Earl of NORTHBROOK pre- sented a bill to amend the Patriotic Fund Act of 1867, and to make certain provision respecting certain funds adminis- tered by the same Commissioners as the Patriotic Fund. Re stated that he would explain the provisions of the bill on the second reading on Thursday night.—The bill was read a first time. RKFORISMK)RT INSTITUTIONS (IRELAND) BILL.—Lord EMILY moved the second reading of this bill, the object of which, he said, was to assimilate the law as to reformatory instittitions in Ireland to that already existing in England and Scotland, and to require the local bodies to contribute towards their construction and improvement. The bill would also enable the Board of Works to Vend money for the 'construction and enlargement of these buildings. The Irish Office, the Board of Works, and the Treasury were all in favour of the bill, therefore he hoped their Lordships would give it a second reading.—The bill was read a second time.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.—Moretetv. Tun REVOLUITONARY CONGRESS. Mr. BELLINGHAM asked whether the Government, as the defenderoof law and , order, were prepared to prohibit such exhibitions as the I , recent revolutionarrcosgress fer the future?—The Home i SECRETARY replied that when any persons,dav speech or Iteriting, incited to crime, whether at home or-abroad, it was ' the duty of the Government to invoke the law for the ' punishment of the offenders. Further thanikat they could , not wisely or safely go.—Mr. BELLINGHAM • asked whethec people had not been imprisoxed in Ireland for using far less violent language.--Sir W. HARCOURT : According to my ' belief and knowledge, no man has been imprisoned in Ireland except in accordance with the law. (Laughter and cries o 4" Oh.") THE DISCOVERY OF 'ETERNAL MACIHNES.—Lord SAN- DON baying asked if the Government could corroborate the , report of the discovery of infernal machines at Liverpool.— Sir W. HARCOURT, in reply, stated that the accounts were substantially correct. The right hon. gentleman added that the Government had not been anxiouWto give publicity to ' the matter, because the knowledge of the fact might have proved an obstacle to Cie detection Of the offender, and be- Cause they did not wish to create an alttrm. Sir W. liar- court proceeded to lay before the House an authoritative account of the discovery and the proceedings taken in con- sequence. It appears that upon therGovernment receiving information of the consignment Of the infernal machines to Liverpool, a confidential agent ntthe Customs and a metro- politan police officer were despatohed to Liverpool to await the arrival of the vessels which had been designated. When they reached the port the cargoes were searched. In the first vessel six machines were 'discovered in a barrel said to contain cement, and in the second vessel four machioes were found concealed in the same manner. The ten boxes • eathoontained a ci,arge of over..2lb. of a highly explosive material, and it was impossible to estimate the fatal effects of even an accidental concussion on such a mass of explo- itive -material. The designs, raid the Home Secretary, appeared upoes the face of tbernto be the precise and literal fulfilment ,of projects openly avowed and declared in the lkish•Fenian Tress of America, Week by week for the last nine months open threats and ,public invitations to general 'outrage and personal assassination had been circulated in • these papers, subscriptions had been openly collected, and 'more than one attempt of the kind had been made in Eng- land by miscreants hired and despatched from America for the parpoee. In his opinion it was the duty of every civilised Government to co-operate in putting down with a strong haled these nefarione enterprises. It was his ,belief that the Government of the United States was ready to punish the authors of each a crime, but in any event her Majesty's Government were fully alive to their responsibility in the matter, and they confidentlycounted on the support of Parliament and the country whilst they employed every power of the executive and everrengiiie of the law to detect and destroy these associations of assassination. TRE TRANSVAAL I/seam—Sir M. HICKS-BEACH brought forward his motion of censure, and the House was then tolerably well attended on both sides, though by no means crowded in any part save in the strangers' galleries. The peers assembled over the clock in great force. Directly Sir M. Hicks-Beach rose a considerable exodus occurred, and after he had been up a few minutes few Irish members were to be seen, and wide gaps were visible on the tenches be- hind him. Liberals, however, remained to keep Ministers inoonotenance, and found several unexpected opportanities of expressing approval of the Government policy by applauding observations which had been intended by Sir Michael Hicks-Beach to be accepted as severe sarcasm. The gravamen of his charge was that the Govern- ment had failed to continue the policy of the late Govern- ment, but his indictment was discursive, often forced, and showed at many points that be had by no means recovered from his annoyance at being obliged at last to submit a resolution which he had during so many months held in terroremover the leads of Her Majesty's Government. The strong point of the right hon. baronet was prophecy, and he predicted awful things in the future, while he won the ap- plause of Mr. Alderman Fowler by his "happy thought" of championing the cause of the fe"natives." By theconclusion of his harangue, which lasted an hour and a half, the assem- blybotb, upstairs and down had diminisieed, and Baron H. de WORMS addressed a still smaller , audienee.—Mr. Baru- mown, beginning with a modest disclaimer of all pretensions' to eloquence, enforced his amendment in a most effective speech, which amounted to a forcible enunciation of the principle that nations should rely on justice mintier than force, which while it scandalised certain ,old .colonels obtained the emphatic favour of the Pdinisterialists and the marked approval of Mr. Gladstone, who, when Mr. liathhone -sat doiniel: turned round on the Treasury benehenopenly offerehint theilke pndoongratula- tion.—After waiting to hear both sides fully, Mr. Caesarea- Lem intervened to give the reply of the Government, and in the course df an hour placed their case very .calmly and conclusively before the House not yet full. Point by point the President of the Board of Trade took up the accusations against the Government, and met them fairly and fully, the gist of his defence of the retrocession of the Transvaal being that in the end we could not have retained it without posi- tive oppression, rind, above all, that "a great nation could afford to be generous." Such views officially announced gave vast offenowto the Tories, and excited the scorn of the members of the Fourth Party in an especial degree, Before he finished Mr. Chamberlain developed positive animation, and dealt some hard knocks at Sir M. Hicks-Beach and those others " who take delight in being humiliated." Mr. Chamberlain was succeeded by Mr. Gorst, to whom fol- lowed Mr. A.ll. Sullivan. A few remarks from Sir Walter Barttelot, not quite, accurately representing a chance re- mark from Mr. Chamberlain called Mr Gladstone up a little earlier than Was expected. He did not waste many remarks on die gallant hammy but, turning to Sir Michael Hicks-Beach, compliniented him npon the more moderate tone adopted in the House ateconipared with what he used outside. Reading a,paragraph from a speech delivered at .Cheltenham, in which the right hon. baronet had declared that no proposale for peace had been made till after three defeats, he asked whether that wee correctly reported.—Sir Michael Hicks-Beach admitting the general accuracy a the report, Mr. Gladstone said, amid loud cheers, "Then I say there is not the slightest foundation for it." He proceeded to abate, as Mr. Chamberlain bad done, that the peace pro- Pouts blidleen madeceacertain conditions before the suc- cesses Pt the Beers„and that those conditions, eteadfaatly adhered; te, had been conceded by the Boers. As to the question of vindicating, the Queen's an- *thy; he declared that' the Government had done everything to vindicate the Queen's authority, except the shedding of more blood. The. Queen's authority had ig foenarmdep,ly vindicated be the assembling of an overwhelm- fully equipped, who could have crushed the Boers ist a short campaign. The Premier's speech, listened to with PaOlound attention bia crowded House, was during the first half rudely and coma ntly interrupted by a little band of members on the baek Conservative benches, prominent anteing them being**. Warten. After bearing with great Patience this unprecedented conduct—imprecedented except in similar circumstances in the present Parliament—the Leader of the Howse appealed to the protection of the pßeaket, an appeal backed up by a prolonged and angry Cheer from the Ministerial benches, which had so much effect that the Speaker did not find it necessary to interfere. lAt one o'clock the Premier resumed his seat amid en- thuniastic cheering from the Liberals, who at this hour filled Up every seat to the right of the Speaker, and overflowed 214t0 the galleries.—Sir S. If not convenient, he would give notice of the question. Sir CHARLES DILHE desired that notice might be given. Tnu LAND BILL.—The House was occupied all day on the " report "of the Land Bill. At the outset new clauses were introduced by the Attorney-General, providing, among other things, that the Commissioners and Assistant Com- missioners shall not be permitted to sit in Parliament during their tenure of office. Several clauses moved by private members were either ruled out of order or negatived, and the rest of the morning sitting was spent in making amendments to the clauses, wl ich were mostly of a Yhrbal and un- important character. At seven o'clock the House was engaged on Clause 4. At the evening sitting, the House pro- ceeded with the bill, but no point of controversy arose until Clause 6, when the Arronnur-Guternar. moved an amend- ment securing to tenants who erect flax-scutching mills their valae as improvements. This was resisted, and carried on a division by 182 to 99. On Clause '7, empowering the Court to fix fair rents, Lord E. Frrenatratou moved an amendment confining the benefit of the clause to tenancies valued under £lOO. In support of this proposal which be said would j only exclude 13,000teuants, he urged the expediency of not I making this exceptional legislation broader than was Neces- sary, and quoted the authority of Lord Carlingford and Mr. Baron Dowse for the proposition that these large tenants I were quite able to take care of themselves. It was energeti- cally opposed by ?QT. GratinsToNE, who pointed out that no 'ouch recommendation had been made by either of the Corn- missions, andaleclared that the Government woald be no parties to drawing a distinction which was directly opposed to the lines on .which the Bill was drawn.—Mr. BRAND replied to this that such a distinction was already drawn in the 16th clause, which allowed tenants of £l6O to contract themselves out of the Bill altogether.—Mr. Lalor, Mr. Collings, and Lord E.. Cavendish spoke against the amend- ment, which was supported by Mr. W. H. Smith and Mr. W. Cartwrigbt. On a division it was negatived by 241 to 205,andthe narrowness of the majority was greeted with loud cheers. Some other amendments were disposed of, and ultimately the debate was adjourned. ROME'OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY. THE 'basil LAND BlLL.—Amidst the applause of Mr. Warton and the laughter of the House, Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL gave notice of his intention to move, as an amendment to the third reading of the Irish Land Bill, a resolution condemning the measure as the result of a revolutionary agitation, and as dangerous to individual freecom.—ln the early part of the afternoon there were dis- cussions on the questions of absenteeism, emigration, fair Tents, and ejectment. Later in the day an interesting and important question arose.—Mr. W. H. SMITH proposed to amend the clause which relates teethe incorporation of the 'Land Commission. It was forand that as the bill stood it would be necessary at the end of seven years to come to Parliament again to continue the appointment of the Com- missioners other than the Judicial Commissioner, and the object of Mr. Smith's proposal was to avoid the necessity for such a etep.—Mr. GLADSTONE thanked the right hon. gentlemen, the member for Westminster, for his suggestion, and said the Government would accept the amendment.— Mr. PARNELL, however, objected, and moved the adjourn- ment of the debate.—The &maxim pointed out that it WAS doubtful whether at that stage a provision of the kind could be considered, as it involved a positive charge upon the people. The point was considered of such importance that Mr. Salm undertook to move the recommittal of the bill with a view to Antving the amendment Weeded; but ALS PREMIER said be could eet agree to the delay of the bill.—Sir S. Nortruccrn • %id the amendment was of such a character that it cow • not be ierodoced in the House of Lords, and if nothing wore done they would have to have another Land Bill at the nd of seven years. The House ought therefore to-consider whether it should not take the step of recommitting the bill upon the third reading rather than be subject to serious inconvenience otherwise. --Mr. PARNELL'S motion and Mr. SMITH'S amendment were then withdrawn. When the time arrived for the adjourn- ment of the House the consideration of the report had pro- ceeded as far as clause 44, leaving 10 clauses to be dealt with before the report stage is completed.—Mr.thunsTorso. stated that he did not anticipate that these would take long, and if the question of recommitting the bill in order to consider Mr. Smith's amendment, was disposed of at an early hour the next day, he should propose immediately afterwards to move the third reading of the bill.—Sir S. NonrucerrE remarked , that there was every disposition on the part of the Opposition to accept the proposal, assuming that the report was concluded at a reasonable hour. The Alkali Works Regulation Bill was read a third time, and the Vivisection Abolition Bill was withdrawn. HOUSE OF LORDS.—THIIRSDAY. .

_ THE REDUCTION OF THE NATIONAL DPBT.

_ MR. GLADSTONE'S SCIIEME. A Treasury minute was issued on Weill446ii explaining the actual operation of Mr. Gladstone's beheiss for, the reduction of the National Debt. He will , ask Parliament to empower him to cancel two millions in annuities held by the National Debt on the ommissioners giving in return the Three per Cent. Perpetual Stock, this stock to be again converted into terminable annuities expiring in 1908. This will give him a margin of £1,540,240, by the aid of which he proposes to cancel stock to the amount of sixty millions. Taking the price of stock at par, the net increase of the charge conQequent upon replacing stock ov annuity will only be £38,364, which will be defrayed out of the New Sinking Fund. The £60,0u0,000 will be obtained, one-third from the !National Debt Commissioners, and the remainder [ from the Chancery Paymaster.

div.head: SiAIE OF IRELAND.
div.p: SiAIE OF IRELAND.

Mr. J. R. Justice, a magistrate, was on Tuesday fined £4 at Rivet:nom dessions for having assaulted a labourer. The labourem' strike in County Cork is already drawing to a close. Phough gangs of labourers still parade some of the country districts, demanding higher wages, this is to be attributed to the fact of their having been late in the field. Those who originated the agitation have resumed work the farmers on the advice of the Land League, having granted their demand. A large body of military and police proceeded from New Ross on Tuesday to aid the sheriff in evicting a woman named Holden from her farm at Shanbough, County Kilkenny. The house was found to be barricaded, and when the door was at last forced great resistance was made by those inside with pitchforks, arc. The people at last surrendered and were arrested, information being sworn on the spot. The five men who were in custody at Tmlee, charged with shooting a bailiff near Castle Island, were finally dis- charged on Saturday, for want of evidence. Two of the witnesses were ordered to be prosecuted for committing perjury. At Bellyfamon, near Carrick-on-Shannon, on Saturday, 48 persons were charged with riot at Readne. where 800 per- sons assembled to cut the turf of Patrick Lynch, a local sus- pect, and afterwards made a threatening demonstration. They were bound over to keep the peace. At the weekly meeting of the Loughrea Guardians, on Saturday, Major Rogers refusing to receive applications from the families of persons arrested under the Coercion Act, 25 guardians left the board-room, and protested against this course. Some of the farmers in county Cork have agreed to give their labourers an advance of wages. It is stated that the labourers in the Greenagh district, who are to have an in- crease of is. per week, have hitherto been paid only 3s. per week, with a "house" free. Five families who were evicted from Colonel Hare's estate at Doon, county Limerick, last week, have remained ever since sitting by the roadside, where they cook their meals during the day, sleeping in neighbouring farmers' houses during the night. They threaten to continue this until re-instated. Two hundred men from the North of Ireland arrived on Monday, at Waterford, and proceeded by steamer te New Noss, escorted by a large body of police, to cut the hay on the estate of Mr. Boyd, who has been "Boycotted" since the committal of two men named Phelan for the murder of his son and an attempt to murder himself. Mr. Boyton, the " suspect " who claimed American citizenship, has been pronounced by his medical attendant to be in a dangerous state of health, and a report will be at once made to the authorities by the medical officer of Kil- mainham Gaol. Mr. Boyton, along with some other pri- soners, has refused to sign a document stating—" I hereby undertake, if released, not to commit any treasonable prac- tice, or commit any act of violence or any intimidation against any of Her Majesty's subjects, or in any manner, directly or indirectly, to incite others to the commission of any such act, and I shall be liable to be re-arrested if I fail to comply with this undertaking." A large number of agents of the Property Defence Asso- ciation arrived in Cork, on Wednesday, to take charge of the vacant farms. Mr. John O'Connor, secretary of the Cork Land League, who was arrested under the Coercion Act, was removed by a strong military and police escort from Naas Gaol to Kil- mainham, on Wednesday morning.

div.head: IRON AND 613-AL TRADES.
div.p: IRON AND 613-AL TRADES.

BARROW-IN-FURNESS, Monday.—The iron market in this district remains in a steady position, and a fair trade is being done in all qualities of metal. The demand is stronger from America and the Continent, and the whole of the yield of the furnaces is now going directly into consumption, and at ithe same time deliveries are so heavy that stocks which re- present a heavy weight of metal are being redaced in a ratio Iwhich gives good hope for the future. More iron is being shipped now than at any previous period of the year, and 'steel is also given into delivery in heavy parcels. Iron ship- builders are very busily employed, and one or two orders of magnitude have come to hand. Iron ore steady, but quiet. Coal and coke in large consumption. LA/M1.5E1E9, WEDNESDAT.—The coal trade of this die- trict continues without material change either as regards prices or demand. Business still drags on in a dull, de- pressed manner through the summer season, and for the present little or no improvement can be looked for. Colliery proprietors, realising that in the present condition of the market concessions in prices have no appreciable effect in increasing the actual amount of trade to be done, are genet.- ' ally showing little orno disposition to press sales at lower prices than those which have been ruling of late, and although the market is weak for the time being, with needy sellers forcing stocks at very low figures, , any further material reduction in quoted rates seems scarcely probable. So far as contracts also are concerned, although colliery pro- prietors are renewing them with their regular customers, they are generally disinclined to enter into new engage- ments over anything like long periods. Rouse fire coals continue in very limited demand, and are accumulating in stock rapidly. Of the common classes of round coal rather more seems to have been going into consumption for). iron making and steam purposes, but this has had no appreciable effect upon the large supplies coming into the market, which are still far in excess of requirements. A moderate 'business is reported in gas making coals, and a very decide* stand is being made by colliery proprietors against contracta for any longer period than twelve months. There has beeti' a very fair inquiry during the week for sleek, and sell have been firm ; but engine fuel generally is still tolerab. plentiful. Prices are without quotable change from last week, and at the pit mouth average about as under. The better qualities of house coals, Ss to 85.4; seconds, es to 7s; common round , coal, 448; I ,fid to 55 6d ; burgy, 4s 3d to 45 9d ; good slack, 38 9d to 48 3d and inferior sorts 3s to 3s ed per .ton, A moderate business is being done in coal, for shipmetd+ined eorne oollieries are fairly,busy in thin branch of trade, but slow prices have to be taken, and steatn.coal delivered at Liverpool and °argotl is being quoted at es (id to 78 per ton. In the iron trade business brie been "rather: quiet during the week; but the matket continues firm, With sellers holding for the alight advance which has recently been made in prices. A fair number of inquiries have been made for forward delivery, but very few makers are disposed to go beyond the end of the year. and in some cases they decline to book further for- ward than the next three months. For Lancashire pig iron local makers are firm at their minimum quotations of 44e to; 45s less 21 delivery equal to Manchester, and at theee figures a few sales have been made. In outside brands it moderate business is being done in Lincolnshire at aboOtt late rates, but other sorts still meet with very little inquiry here. In the finished iron trade a very fair improvement seems to be established, and makers thtougbout this district are now generally well employed, with, in some cases. orders in hand for several months to come. Better prices have also been realised npon. new business, £5 17s ed per tot representing the average figure at which local bars have lately been sold for delivery -into the Manchester district, Said makers ate now asking la In the engineering branches Of trade a steadily increasing amount of activity is re- ported, and there are at present fewer men out of employ. rent than has been the case for several years past in this district. THE COMMITTEE ON THE LAND BILL.

CLOSING SCENE. ~ • • A oorrtependent of the Observe, writing" from the Cross Beechen," says-v.—At half-past one o'clock this (Saturday) morning Mr. Gladstone shut up his papers, pulled down his cuffs, tugged violently at the back of his coat, and walked out of the House amid loud cheering from the Minis- terialists. The Land Bill was through committee at last. It was a proud moment in a long and illustrious life--a fresh triumph in a victorious career. Yet so curiously do light and shadow intermingle in this life that the cup of the Premier's joy was dashed with a bitter flavour. He was the victim of those social amenities which he, as a rule, daringly disregards. He had knelt at the altar of fashion, and the great goddess had bestowed upon the unaccus- tomed votary a cruel gift. In plain language, the Premier, dining with the Prince of Wales, had, for the OCCA9IOO, sub- mitted to be inducted into a a new coat, and felt as un- comfortable as David did when he donned the unaccus- tomed armour. If the people did not think Bo much about these trifles. Mr. Gladstone would gladly have carried out .the institution a step further, and taken off his coat, as David cast off his armour; but on reflection he thought he had gone far enough in the direction of sartorial surprises. To sit on the treasury bench balancing on his brow a bat six hizes too small was sufficient for one session. His ap- pearance at the table in his shirt sleeves, while personally ,agreeable and admirably adapted to the work in hand, ;might have led to remark. So the Premier kept the gar- meut on, and wrestled with it as if it were a new clause to the Land Bill proposed by Mr. Chaplin. He tugged at the sleeves, clutched at the collar, and made frantic efforts to achieve impossible things in the direction of fingering the ;seam between his shoulders. It was well Sir Stafford North- cote was out of the way, or that, having arrived somewhat 'late, he meekly took his place on the front bench and at- tempted to look as if he were not there. At a single word the Premier would have bounded upon him, and flung him on one side. But Sir Stafford had gone through this pro- cess on Thursday night, and was not inclined for a repeti- tion. So with. hands meekly folded up his sleeves .and ,knees tightly held together he sat quiescent.
