div.head: EXTRAORDINARY FENIAN CONSPIRACY. DascovEßY OF INFERNAL MACHINES AT LIVERPOOL.
div.p: EXTRAORDINARY FENIAN CONSPIRACY. DascovEßY OF INFERNAL MACHINES AT LIVERPOOL.

t The Liverpool correspondent of the Press Association : says: What would appear to be the most extensive plot i ever arranged by the Feoians for the destruction of public buildings in England, has happily been frustrated by the r care and watchfulness of the Custom House authorities and l the detective police of Liverpool. For some time past it t has been suspected that a considerable traffic in explosives ; had been carried on between America and this country, : throitgli the agency of certain people in Liverpool who are I not licensed to deal in such commodities. Recently more detailed information was received, which caused a sharp ! look-out to be kept on all goods arriving from the United , States at Liverpool. Major Grieg, the head of the Liver- pool police, and Chief-Superintendent Williams, of the detective department, were entrusted with the inquiries, and Mr. Gardener, head Collector of Customs at Liverpool, was also specially commissioned by Sir Charles Duncan, chair- man of the Board of Customs, to closely watch all arrivals of goods, and generally to investigate the matter. The re- ports received were to the effect that by one .of the largest vessels of one of the principal lines of steamers sailing be- tween the United Statesand Liverpool, a number of infernal machines, loaded with dynamite, were being conveyed to , this country. Several vessels were searched, but without any result. On the arrival of the Malta, belonging to the Cunard line, however, one particular portion of her cargo aroused suspicion. This was a consignment of a number of barrels of eement, an article which coming to Liverpool somewhat resembles receiving coals at Newcastle. These barrels were detained, awl in order to keep the matter as secret as possible it was decided to ex- amine them in the middle of the night. The examination took place in one of the wharfs at the linakission Dock, none but Custom House officers being present. Six or seven of the barrels were opened without anything being found, but eventually a barrel was opened which afterwards was noticed to have on it a black cross not to be found on the others, and in this were found six zinc boxes, which upon further e.amination proved to be infernal machines with neatly constructed clockwork, and some stuff that looked like dynamite ready prepared. Dr. Campbell Brown was asked to examine this stuff, and pronounced it really to be dynamite. Each box contained about 31b5. of the mixture, one or two of them containing besides a quantity of nitro- glycerine. A clockmaker was called in to examine the machinery, and he stated that the works were of a very simple but effective kind. After being started the machine would run for about six hours, when a portion of the clock- work would move a powerful spring, which would be brought into contact with a percussion-cap, and so the explosive would be fired. During the examination one of the officers incautiously started one of the machines, but the action was of course immediately stopped. The Malta had on board nearly 200 passengers, and it is terrible to think what would have been the result if one of these machines had been started accidentally during the voyage. The Home Secre- tary was communicated with, and one of these machines, the dynamite having previously been extracted, was forwarded to London for examination. A few days after the arrival of the Malta, the Bavarian, one of Ley- land's steamers, having on board some passeng- ers,' but carrying principally cattle, arrived in the same dock. She had on board some barrels of cement con- signed to the same persons. These were, of course, examined, and in one of the barrels six more machines, constructed on the same plan, were found, each of these containing 31b. of explosive metal in one of the barrels. 'lt is stated that 1 some billheads bearing the name "J: O'Donovan Roma " were found, and if this has not been done by the real con- signees to avert suspicion from themselves, it would appear that Roesa's boast that it was through the agency of himself and kis organisation that the Dotterel was destroyed was no empty one. It is unfortunately almost certain that the cul- prits in this matter will escape with impunity. With com- mendable wisdom they have at present made no claims for the "cement." Every inquiry is being made in 'the United States with a view to discover the maker of the.clockworlr, and to generally tracing up full particulars of the matter but beyond the information thus offered to the Home Otflc iand the police here, but little good result can come of a toowl edge. The Customs authorities at Liverpool are stiil 'ton the alert, as several more attempts wil', according to the reports received, be made to import similar infernal machines Into this country. The authorities at Queenstown, d other ports to which vessels sail from America, have 1:Ito been put on their guard. 'By the Explosives Act, 98 d 32 Vic., c. 17, "any person imparting explosives with- out a license is liable to a penalty of £lOO, or six months' is. imprisonment, at the discretion of the justices." The dynamite contained in the machines having been examined, beyond the first examination made by Dr. Brown and one of Her Majesty's inspectors of explosives, was taken out into 30 fathoms of water in a special steamer, and there destroyed.

STATEMENT BY MR. O'DONOVAN ROMA. The New-York correspondent of the Daily News, tele- graphing on Wednesday, says :—Mr. O'Donovan Roses says that as far, as he .is concerned the Liverpool report,of dynamite machines is entirely false. Me: bas not shipped any, knows no one who has, and thinks.ihe story too culous for a sensible person to believe for *moment. If the machines really were found there they were sent as a plot to. create prejudice against those who wish freedom for Ireland. Still it is not improbable that they were sent by Irishmen; judging by the spirit that animatee many of them in America. Australia, and England itself. There is a wide- spread determination among the Irish people, Mr. O'Donovan Rossa says, to teach England that it would be a wise policy to give up the government of Ireland. He declines to answer the question if the Society of United Irishmen is furnishing sabstantial aid to the secret attacks on the British Government.

ST. HELENS POLICE COURT. - FRlDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrieon) and Mr. W. Pilkington. STEALING Offal= FEATHERS.—Ann Bash, an elderly woman, was charged on remand with stealing two ostrich feathers, value 13s 1011, the property of James Pickup, draper, Blackburn.—From the evidence it appeared the pro- secutor kept a stall in the market; and on Monday, being informed that a woman had taken away two ostrich feathers from his stall, he went after the prisoner, who was SOHN yards distant at another stall, and asked her to deliver up the stolen property. One ef the feathers had fallen to the ground and the other was found beneath her cloak. He took her back to his stall, and she began to cry, and said she had ten children to keep. About 300 people assembled around her, and some of them demanded her-release. No polieeman being near at the time, he was unable to give her into cus- tody, and fearing to leave his goodsunprotected he accepted ss, which the woman offered as "compensation for damage to one of the feathers, in the event of his being able to pro- secute her," and allowed her to go.—P.C. Caunce appre- hended the woman shortly afterwards.—Cross-examined by Mr. Swift, who appeared for prisoner, witness said prosecutor informed him that he had received ss, as he was compelled to attend to his business, but this. did not debar him from action. Witness being asked by Mr. Swift if this was said to him the first time he saw the prosecutor, he replied that he did not remember, at which Mr. Swift was very indig- nant, and said the officer ought to be " striPPed."—Supt. Johnston here interposed, and said the question had been answered; and the Bench requested Mr. Swift to conduct his case properly. Mr. Swift said people's liberties were trifled away with evidence of that kind, and then proceeded with his cross-examination.—Prisoner was committed to take her trial at the sessions. MONDAY.—Before Messrs. W. L. Evans and W. Blinkhorn. It:Dacia/ex.—James Johnson, Windle, was charged with indecency with intent to insult certain females, in North- road, on Saturday evening.—Annie Pemberton and Mary Hardy, two domestic servants engaged at a gentleraan's house in North-road, gave evidence in support of the charge.— P.C. Cottam apprehended the prisoner in the Windy Har- bour public-house, and charged him with committing the offence. Prisoner replied, "I am not going with you on i that charge," and attempted to run away.—Prisoner, who denied the charge, and said he had a wife and five children, was sent to prison for a month, with hard labour. A Cumous WITNESS.—John Swift, an elderly man, was charged with being drunk at Rainford, on the 17th July.— Defendant handed to the deputy magistrates' clerk a piece of paper, which he said was a " witness " that he was not drunk. Some amusement was caused on the paper being examined, and found to be "a bill for a pair of boots."— . Fined ss. and costs. YOUNG BATHERS FlNED—Joseph Watkins, James Mandsley, Christopher Lincoln Gardner, and Edward Johnson, boys, were charged with indecently exposing them- selves in a field, off Boundary-road, on the 20th July.—P.C. Young said the boys had been bathing, and were running about in the field—They were let off on payment of the costs (3s. 6dl each), and promising not to offend again. BRUTAL ASSAULT ON A GROCER'S Assurrevr.—Michael Higgins was charged with assaulting and beating Matthew, Highland.—Mr. Swift said complainant, who was one of Mr. Edward Johnson's assistants at his grocer's shop in Parr-street, on Saturday night, at ten minutes to eleven, left the shop to go home, and crossed over the street along with a boy who works in the shop, and Was immediately attacked by four men on the other side of the street. He knew the other three men by eight, but not by name. He knew Higgins both by sight and by name. Complainant was struck and knocked down, very violently beaten, and kicked by all the four. He would establish, he thought, to their worships satisfaction that defendant Higgins was one of the four; in fact the shop boy said to him that he knew him. The shop boy was also struck and knocked lown. The assault was a very violent and unprovoked one, and one was really at a lose to knew what could have induced the assault. Of course, in these days perhaps it was not necessary to account for assaults, as they seemed to be done for secret reasons one could not very well go into in public.—Complainant gave evidence in support of this statement, and exhibited his left eye which appeared to have been violently abused. He was kicked in a most shameful manner, and was sore all over his !body. Ile had been asked to join a secret society—about three months ago—but refused. This was the second time be had been attacked. Cross-examined by Mr. Riley complainant said he had known prisoner about three weeks; a friend named M'Cabe pointed him out as he was passing with some others. 51`Cabe also said that the first attack tbat was made upon him was for spleen in Ireland, and that ' Higgins had said it was not all over yet. He came from Ireland on the 11th August last.—P.C. John Carruthers said he apprehended the prisoner that morning at his lodgings 21, Bolton-street, Parr, and in answer to the charge he said "I do not know the man at all." He then took him to Matthew Highland, who said prisoner was one of the four who had assaulted him. Prisoner then replied, , "No, I was at Widnes on Saturday night."—Mary Clarke, 1 with whom complainant lodges, also gave evidence to the 1 LAST WEEKS effect that complainant was brought home soon after eleven and appeared to have teen badly treated. ROBBERIES.—John Sandford (17) was charged with hav- ing, between the 17th and the 18th April, stolen a pair of boots, shirt, and stockings, the property of Henry Dixon. He was also charged with stealing a pair of trousers. and a petticoat, the property of George Mobberly, horse slaugh- terer, with whom he was employed.—Prisoner was left in charge of Mobberley's house during Mr. and Mrs. Mobber- ley's absence, and on their return they missed the goods.— Prisoner, who pleaded guilty, was sentenced to one month's imprisonment on each charge.—Ellen Carty, married woman, was charged with stealing a shawl and hat, value 25., the property of Mary Broughton on Cropper's Twenty-one days' imprisonment.-2-Jane Waters pleaded guilty to stealing from a stall in the Market, belonging to Mrs. Duggan, a woman's dress and a boy's frock coat, value Bs. 6d.—She was fined ss.

A PIIBLICHOUSE Mertens/4ex. John- Summerfield Eccleston' was charged with being drunk on the licensed premises of William Butter, and refusing to quit.—P.C. Parker said that on the previous evening at half-past six, he was called to the Coffee House Inn, off East-street, to put out the prisoner who was creating a disturbance. He got him out with grest difficulty.—Prisoner pleaded guilty was fined 58. and costs, or seven days' imprisonment. Dentscixo THE CELLS.—Catherine Wynn, keying ane fixed residence, but who admitted having been in prison "a few times," was charged with being drunk, and also with damaging the closet in the police cell doing damage to the extent of 4s.—For being drunk she was ordered to pay ss. and costs or seven days, and the amount of damage, or seven days.

MANCHESTER CORN, Tul:Sanaor.—The strong 1000 in quota- tions for wheat and fiour has again prevailed since last market day, and a considerable amount of business has been transacted. Spring oorn, on the contrary, has 'ailed le.. active. Imports have cdmprLsed average supplies of wheat and flour, liberal of , maize, and fair of .user produce. To-day's market was well attended, but there svas only a moderate business passing. English wheat was scarce and dearer Foreign brought an ad- vance in some instances of Id. per ceutal. Flour also must be quoted Id to 24 per cental higher. Oats sold slowly, Beans and peas were each fully as dear. Maize, with continued liberal shipments, receded Id per cental. MANCHESTER COTTON, TRUESDA Y —Spinners may be, and probably are, painfully conscious of the firmness reported in the cotton market, but it is entirely lost upon buyers of yarn and cloth. They are also firm, but it is at the prices quoted, in limiting their immediate wants to to the smallest possible bounds and making much lower offers than cut rentzates for anything of which they are not in actual need. It is scarcely worth while to add the the, e is little business in progress. LIVERPOOL CORN. THIIRSDAY.—Today the market for wheat Is somewhat firmer. The prices are the same as yesterday. ps flout there is a little doing. Indian corn is generally steady at yesterday's rates; the latest quotations being is 4s Iltd to be for new. LI tie business has been done in Beans and peas at the prices of last "market day. Oats and oatmeal very quiet. LIVERPOOL PROVISIONS, THERSDAY.—Beef quieter. Pork in steady consumptive request. Bacon: & better feeling. Hams fairly active. Shoulders dull or sale. Lard meets but a limited demand, and at somewhat easier figures. Cheese in active re- quest Dotter quiet. LIVERPOOL COTTON, THURSDAY.—Spot. The spot demand continues active, and a large business has again been done at hardening prices. Sales 14,000 bales, including 1,000 on specu- lation or for export. The quotations for American low mid- dling and upwards are raised 1-16 d per lb. Imports since Thursday 27,096 bales, including 18,917 American. Futures have been very strong all day, and prices are 1-16 d for near and 1-32 d for distant positions higher than the top prices of last evening.

CATHOUC SOCIAL. CLIIH.—The members of the Liverpool Catholic Club, which numbers several St. Helens getlemen, had their first annual pic-nic to Knowsley Park, on Tuesday last. This club numbers amongst its members many wealthy Liverpool gentlemen, and premises in Liverpool, known as the Queen's Hotel, have been secured at a cost of £25,000. The members started from the club at one o'clock and went by Knotty Ash, to Knowsley Park, in wagonette. A cold collation was served up in first class style to which about 100 persons sat down. The members afterwards indulged in dancing to the tones of a quadrille band, and a variety of amusements were enjoyed. At seven o'clock tea was provided and the return journey commenced immediately afterwards. Amongst those present were Messrs. J. A. Clarke and Donnelly, of St. Helens; Messrs. F. J. M'Adaue, J. D. Byrne, M'Ardle, J. M. Murphy, Dr. and Mrs. Parsons.

they were—were car, tlessly suffered to stand over. When the present Government began at first to touch them, Lord Salisbury railed at the idea that a concert of the Powers in compelling these stipulations to be fulfilled could be obtained. Spite of his scoffs, however, which were plainly meant to increase the difficulties, Lord Granville and gr. Goschen between them were able both to secure and to preserve the European concert until the Turkish Government, after no end of evasioo and haggling, was obliged to come to terms, and to give up the lands peopled by Greeks and Albanians whioh the Congress of Berlin had decided should be ceded to Greece and Montene- gro. More than once war seemed imminent, during the protracted negociations ; but by superhuman patience and tact on the part of the Governments which took the lead in this business the last obstacle was removed ; and Mr. Goschen on his return to I England is able to tell us that the quarrel between I the Porte and its neighbours is composed ; that the , territories are already handed over or in process of transfer ; in short, that the Eastern Question, for the time being and as to its current phases and exigencies at least, is disposed of. Is not this something for the people of England to rejoice over, and for the Government which has accomplished the task to take due credit for f' In presence of this success, Tory carping in that regard has perforce been dropped. And last comes the quarrel in the Transvaal, manu- factured for us with so much perverted ingenuity by I a Conservative Government and its emissary, Sir Bartle Frere. That was about the ugliest affair Mr. Gladstone's Government had to deal with when it ac- ceded to office. The facts are too notorious now to need repetition. We had gone into a country occupied by a colony of Dutchmen whose independence we had pledged ourselves to respect, and had summarily an- nexed it directly against the wishes of the great majority of the colonists. When they remonstrated, our officials installed in authority there treated their protests with supercilious disdain ; when they or- ganised a formidable revolt, those officials criminally deceived the Government at home by declarations that the disaffected party was insignificant ; and when at length a British General precipitately at- tacked the instil gents, he met with such a hot recep- tion as he had•not reckoned on, and had to recoil in severe defeat. Meanwhile the Government at home which had come in uncommitted to the wrongful act id annexation, had received convincing evidence that the Boers were united in the purpose to recover their independence ; and that Government, in harmony with the declara- tions of its chief members when out of office, took the resolution to restore self-government to those Dutch colonists; and were not deterred frotn continuing the negociations which had commenced through the friendly mediation of the President of the Orange Free State, by the untoward repulse of the same fool- hardy general who had been defeated before, in a second assault upon the defensive position of the in- surgent colonists. The negociations had ended in the concessions of internal self-rule to the Transvaal Boers, under a British suzerainty including control of foreign affairs. These, in briefest statement, were the main facts upon which the debate turned on Mon- day night. The Opposition made a feeble fight of it; and Mr. Gladstone, Mr. Chamberlain, and Mr. Rath- bone, in their very powerful speech( s, triumphantly vindicated the Government's policy in making an early and honourable peace with the Boers, and re- ceived the endorsement of the House of Commons by a great majority of 109 votes on a division. Thus closes with a signal victory for the Government the controversy on the last of the three main branches of their foreign policy at which we have retrospectively glanad.

THE appointment of assistant overseer for the township of Whiston, which was made at the last meeting of the Prescot Board of Guardians, appears to have created a considerable amount of feeling amongst the ratepayers. It was stated at a meeting of ratepayers that a memorial signed by gentlemen I—presenting three-fourths of the rateable value of the township, was presented to the board of guardians on the subject, but that the memorial was never read or even looked at. This statement Wag not denied at the board meeting on Thursday. There cannot be a doubt that the appointment rests entirely with the board of guardians, and that they can elect whom they please, subject to the approval of the Local Government Board, but when such an influential memorial as this was presented to the guardians, it says but little for their courtesy when they accord it such scanty consideration. During the lively discussion which took place on the subject at the meeting of the guardians on Thursday last, the Chairman gave utterance to a statement which has completely taken us by surprise. He questioned whether an election was ever carried on honestly and straight-forward, and said that "if every man would only tell the truth from the commence- ment to the termination, you would find that the greatest hypocrisy is carried on." If Mr. Marsh intended his remarks to apply to all public boards then we must take exception to them, as we believe from our knowledge of members of public bodies, extending over a considerable period, and a very wide area, that these gentlemen do act honestly and straightforward as a rule. But on the other hand if his remarks were only applicable to the Prescot Board of Guardians, we must admit that as Mr. Marsh has presided over that body for a number of years, he has had ample opportunity of seeing the inner workings of the board and ought to know what he is talking about. The statement, certainly conveys a serious reflection upon the integrity of the guardians generally, which we think they can scarcely afford not to notice. If it is true that the Prescot Board of Guardians are guilty of hypocrisy—for that is what their chairman says—in conducting their elections, then we do not wonder at the ratepayers of Whiston protesting against the actions of the board and laying the whole of the circumstances before the Local Government Board, who are not likely to countenance anything of that kind. Our public men should be above suspicion, and if they do not faith- fully and honestly carry out the trust reposed in them, the sooner they are replaced by those who will do so ID an upright and straightforward manner, the better it will be for the community.

div.head: LOCAL NOTES.
div.p: LOCAL NOTES.

I came across a very amusing instance of the progress of high life in the kitchen this week. A lady and gentleman, about to leave home for a few weeks, confided the care of their house to the servant and an old housekeeper, whom they specially engaged to supervise matters during their absence. A couple of days after their departure, the servant's mother arrived, and immediately installed herself in the house, oc- cupying and receiving any friends that called upon her ia the drawing-room. When a fortnight had passed by the housekeeper in charge mildly mentioned to the servant that her mother was making rather a long visit. "Oh, it's all right," somewhat indignantly returned the damsel, " When missas comes back I mean to tell her that my mother has been staying here and pay for her board."

We are evidently on the eve of effecting a great change in our means of locomotion. The tricycle is getting so much into favour that the police have need it very successfully in capturing thieves and escaped prisoners. This week I heard of a Benedict whose conduct is worthy of imitation. This gentleman has just started upon a week's tour through the country, accompanied by his partner for weal or woe, upon a double tricycle. When we consider how much of the work of propelling would be likely to fall to his share, I do not think that this can be regarded as a mean act of husbandly devotion. Probably we may soon hear of large family con- veyances being constructed on the tricycle system, for already they are being made to accommodate three persons.

Building societies are not quite strangers to our town, and I was pleased to read the remarks of Dr. McNicol on thrift and building societies in general. The doctor believes that the economical bumps in the heads of our English working classes would do with a little cultivation, and in this I agree with him, and especially so as regards the workingclassesin our own town. The virtue of thrift is neglected, drunkenness and feasting is prevalent Nhen the wages have been got hold of, qmi then there is semi-starvation until the weekly wages arrive again, unless the shopkeeper is bamboozl,d and an account run up which may never be wiped off. lam glad to say that this description is not applicable to all the working classes, but there is an abun- dance of deplorable evidence that it is true regarding a sub- stantial portion et them; and all the efforts made to induce them to provide an umbrella fer the storm deserves our most earnest encouragement.

The evidence in the case of Mary Clark and William Jones, which was heard at the Warrington police court on Friday, revealed not only some sharp practice, but also a curious way of levying a distress. Clark had been a tenant of Mr. Thornton's at Cockhedge, and as she owed 3s. 9d. for rent a bailiff was instructed to levy an eascution upon her goods. Mrs. Clark, however, thought she would keep the bailiff outside, but that worthy being armed with a warrant, believed he had a right to get in how he pleased, and so effected an entrance through the bedroom win- dow. This was certainly a novel way to en, er a debtor's house, and I scarcely think that Mr. Jones will be upheld by any of our legal authorities in allowing his zeal for his employers to carry him to such lengths. Jones thus being a trespasser on Clarke's premises, he need not have been surprised that she "laid about him with the poker," "a marmalade pot," and "pieces of loose flags," to his injury. Thinking, however, to get redress for the in- juries he received, whilst thus seizing Clarke's furniture, he summoned her to the police court, but on arrival there the whole facts came out, and it was stated that Clarke was badly used by Jones and his assistant, who dragged her from one room to another and struck her a blow with a poker. If the latter statement was correct I should think that these two men must have felt that they were acting in a very manly manner thus to attack a woman. The magistrates, however, to the bailiff's intense chagrin, took a common sense view of the cabe and in dis- missing the summons ordered Jones to pay the costs, rema k- ing that it was a great shame that the woman should have been treated with such sharp practice, seeing that she was only one week in arrear with her rent.

I suppose we shall 1300 n have some of the Irish agitators here. Miss Jessie Cregan, a Scotch lady, is about to be sent by the Land League round England to "agitate." Soon we shall have more agitators than agitated. The lady is said to be very comical ;—this I can vouch for. It is also said that she can always contrive to put her audiences into a good temper before letting them hear the" painful truth ;" —this I cannot vouch for. I can, however, assure my readers that she does not scruple to use some very strong la ngaage. FLaCCUS

WIDNES WESLEYAN METHODISTS, OAKLAND -STREET. —The friends connected with this plaee of worship had an excursion to Tranmere on Saturday, in the steamer Kings- town. The weather was of a rather unfavourable character.

COLLEGE OP PRECEPTORS' EXAMINATION.—The follow- ing boys from Cambridge School, Sale, have passed, each in eight subjects, viz., H. Symes and W. Duncan, in the 2ndl division of the second class ; and J. D. Morton, in the let division of the third class. RUNCORN STARR- BOWICETT Eintranstn SOCIETY.—The first subscription meeting of this society was held on Mon- day evening, at the Public Hall, when there was a good attendance, and a number of new shares were taken up. RUNCORN MERSEY MISSION EXCURSION.— On Monday the scholars and friends connected with the Runcorn Mersey Mission to Seamen had an excursion to Grappenhall, under the leadership of Mr. Shaw, the active missionary. They were taken in two boats and were accompanied by the drum and fife band. The weather was of a propitious character, and the party had a capital day's enjoyment. WIDNES ODDEELLOWS.—On Monday afternoon the members of the Widnes Loyal Royal Oak lodge of Odd- fellows, Manchester Unity, celebrated their anniversary. About noon a precession was formed in the principal street, and the members, headed by the band of the training ship ndef atigable, and the banner of the lodge, marched through he town, attracting considerable attention. They after- wards had a tea at the Volunteer Hall. RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUMORITY.—The fort- nightly meeting was held on Tuesday at Dutton Workhouse, Mr. Mclntyre presiding. There were also present Messrs. John Ashton, Charles Reynolds, John Darbvshire, J. Mid. wood, and W. Jackson. The Clerk presented a report of the Frodsham water scheme, which was referred to a committee of Guardians and ex-officio Gaardians of Frodsham and Frodsham Lordship. Mr. Joseph Wilkinsrn, of Muston, was appointed as clerk of works of the Frodaham sewerage works. On the motion of Mr. Charles Reynolds, i• was decided that urban powers be asked for in respect of Fred- sham and Frodsham Lordship. THE SAD ACCIDENT TO A YOUNG MAN AT WIDNES.— Mr. C. E. Driffield, county coroner, held an inquest at the Mersey Hotel, Widnes, on Saturday afternoon, on the body of a young man named James Oakes, 17 years of age, who died on the previous Wednesday evening, at the Hospital, as the result of injuries sustained whilst working at Messrs. Hay, Gordon, and Co.'s chemical works.—Sarah Oakes, widow and mother of deceased ; Frederick Lowe, Dundalk- lane, Ditton, a horse driver at the works where deceased was employed; a workman named Smith, and Miss Janet Downey, matron at the hospital, were examined. The evi- dence was of a similar nature to that reported in the last issue of The Examiner. We may add that deceased had been in the employ of the firm about a month, and had Iprior to that been a farm labourer. The statements of the witnesses showed that his death was accidental, and the jury returned a verdict to this effect. RUNCORN BETHESDA CONGREGATIONAL SUNDAY SCHOOL—On Tuesday, 250 of the young folks connected with this school, and a few friends, including the Rev. T. D. Thomas, the pastor; Mr. Wm. Handley and Mr. Fair- hurst, left Runcorn by the 12-15 p.m. train for Sutton Weaver. From the station they proceeded to Mr. Wilkin- son's farm, Aston, and that gentleman placed afield at their disposal. Various games were engaged in until about half- past three in the afternoon. The elder members of the com- pany then adjourned to the large dairy on the farm, whet.° tea was provided; and the children also had tea in the field. The return journey was commenced at about eight o'clock, so that the company arrived in Runcorn at a com- paratively early hour.

SERIOUS SAFE ROBBERY AT RUNCORN.—About four o'cloc on Monday afternoon, between £5O and £6O, of which about £4O was in gold, was stolen from a Miler's safe at the Fleetwood Arms, Church-street, kept by Mr. George Saunders. The landlord states that about four o'clock in the -afternoon he left the bar, in which the safe was with the keys in the lock, and went into the kitchen which is about ten yards away, to have his tea with the members of his family. At this time there was a man sitting in the bar, and on return- ing, in about 14 minutes, he found that the money had been taken out of the safe, and the man was gone. Information was at once given to the police, who locked up a stranger on suspicion, but he was afterwards discharged, there being no evidence against him. On the following mornin,r, the out- side case of the cash-box, and two bank books belonging to the landlord, were found at the back of Mr. Booth's house. Waterloo-road, by a lad, and given to Mrs. Booth. They were afterwards handed to the police, who made a careful search, and were successful in finding the inside of the cash box near the same place.

A WIDNES CAPTAIN DROWATED.—THE CORONER ON TEE MORTUARY QUESTION.—On Thursday afternoon, Mr. Ridgway, county coroner, held an inquiry at the Boat- house Inn, Runcorn, on the body of Jesse Jones, of White- street, Widnes, captain of the flat May, belonging to Messrs. Allen, Green, and Co., of Liverpool, who was drowned on Tuesday night, in the river Mersey, near Messrs. Brandrit's shipbuilding yard. Previous to the commencement of the inquiry, mr. Ridgway said he bad received information to the effect that the new mortuary at the cemetery was now ready for the re mption of dead bodies, and he asked Mr. W. Handley, the foreman of the jury, whether arrankements had been made for inquests being held there.—Mr. Handley said he understood that inquests would in future be held at the office of he cemetery.—The Coroner remarked that as the law was very strict on matters of this nature, he should like to know whether the matter could be brought under the the notice of the Burial Board, so that they might decide to pass a resolution authorising the use of the room for that purpose whenever it might be required.—Mr. Hand- ley said he woald see the chairman of the Burial Board (Mr. Coleburn) about the matter, and ask him to bring it forward at the next rneeting —The evidence was of a very simple character, and to the effect that deceased was about 29 years of age, and he had left a wife and three children. On Tuesday night, he left his vessel, in company with David Jones, a sailor on the same boat, who lives in Church-street, Widnes, for the purpose of having a walk. Whilst they were going along, they met another man who was known to the deceased, and the three went into a pub- lic-house near the Runcorn railway bridge. They each had four glasses of beer, and left about half-past ten. Jones went with deceased to the pier near Brundrits' yard, and in order to get upon his own vessel he had to walk across the deck of a packet which was lying close to the side of the river. Having parted with deceased, Jones went on his way home, bat he had only got about ten yards when he heard a splash and a noise as if a man were in the water. He ran 13c,t and called to the captain of a schooner, and threw the deceased a rope, but as it was very dark they could not see him, and he was drowned. Deceased was "as sober as could be "on getting to the vessel, and the only explanation %Wei the witness Jones could give of the mishap was that deceased must have missed his footing when upon the Paddle. The body VMS found on the following morning by Charles Lucas, shipwright, Ashbridge-street, in water which was about nine feet in depth. ACCIDENT AT WIDNES.—On Monday evening, a married man named James Brandwood, employed as a salt- cake man at Messrs. Gaskell and Deacon's works, met with .an accident of a serious nature. He was drawing the fire out of his furnace, when a large quantity of hot cinders fell into the ash-hole. This caused the hot water in the ash- pan to splash upon him and badly scald his arms and chest. He was taken to the Hospital. PRESENTATION TO AN ORGANIST AT RUNCORN.—On Tuesday evening last, Mr. Charles Pownall, who is organist, choirmaster, and Sunday school teacher at the Newtown Missio.. Church, was presented with a very hand, some timepiece by the teachers and friends connected with the Mission (on his approaching marriage) in recognition of the esteem in which he is held by them. The presentation took place at the house of Mr. Wainwright, librarian to the Sunday school, in consequence of the Mission undergoing re-decoration, and we are ti:Jry to state that the subscribers to the presentation ceuld not be invited, on account of this utforseen occurrence. Several of the teachers were present, when the Rev. T. D. Simpson (ir the absence of the Rev. Canon Barclay) made the presentation, and in a brief speech alluded to the number of years Mr. Charles Pownall had been connected with the Mission Church, and the musical ability he had displayed in training the choir to the high standard it had attained, and hoped that he would be long spared to carry on the work he is now engaged in. Mr. Pownall, in reply, thanked the teachers and friends for the handsome present, and said that it would always give him pleasure to do what he possibly could for the welfare of the Newtown Mission Church. Antr a few remarks from one or two:of the teachers the meeting was brought to a close.

RE Jose PASSIM'S BartitstrPrcrr.—The case of John Passey, bankrupt, of Anne-street, Widnes, came before Mr. J. F. Collier, judge, at the Liverpool Bankruptcy Court, yesterday. Mr. Lupin, barrister, said that on the 6th July 1874, the liquidating debtor gave a bill of sale over his furniture and household effects in Widnes. The document was registered on the 17th July the same year, in favour of Mr. Johnson, grocer, who seized the goods under it, in March last year, a day or two before the bankrupt filed Lis petition, which was done on the 15th March, 1880. The trustee in liquidation at once gave notice to Mr. Johnson, warning him that the petition had been filed, and that he should hold him responsible for any loss In defiance of that notice Johnson insisted upon selling the goods, and on the 16th March he disposed of them, and realised upon them £29 Sc. 5d., after paying expenses. Mr. Lupin now asked that the sum in question might be paid over to the trustee. In the first place, the bill of sale registered on the 17th July, 1874, had never been re-registered, which should have been done in the ordinary course of things, on or before the 17th July, 1879. The trustee had made an affidavit stating that the said Edward Johnson had neglected to re-register the bill of sale, and it was, therefore, void. Mr. Johnson only took a formal possession of the goods.—Mr. Swift (who appeared for Mr. Johnson): Pardon me, but my friend is bound by the file and by the affidavits, and the affidavits do not say one single word about formal possession.—His Honour: So it appears to me. —Mr. Lupin submitted that he was entitled to call witnesses to show that Mr. Johnson was only in formal possession.— His Honour remarked that what Mr. Lupin wished to show was. that the affidavits had not stated the matter correctly. —Mr. Swift: They have really had 18 months—froin the 15th of March last year—in which to get up their else.— Mr. Lupin said he would go to the real point, viz., that the consideration was not really properly stated in the bill of sale.—Mr. Swift maintained that the matter referred to by Mr. Lupin applied to bills of sale executed after the passing of the last Act dealing with them, and not to a bill of sale executed in 1874 —Mr. Lupin : Thedebtor admits that the consideration is not properly stated in the bill of sale.—His Honour (to Mr. Lupin): You are out or order there again, because there is no notice to refer to the debtor's evidence. —Mr. Swift: Quite so.—Mr. Lupin : You will adjourn the case?—Mr. Swift: What, after this lapse of time 7—The Judge: You must file another motion stating the thing for consideration.—Mr. Swift: It would be much better to dis- pose of this motion altogether.—Mr. Lupin: I do not think it will make any difference to the other side.—Mr. Swift: It is clear that this motion has only been brought for the sake of costs—nothing else.—Mr. Lupin: That I entirely repudiate.—An adjournment was then agreed to.

EDDISBURT PETTY SESSIONS.—On Monday, William Robinson, late part proprietor of Cuddington Mills, was charged with a series of assaults upon his wife. The evidence of the complainant showed that the defendant bad lately given way to drinking, and on several occasions he had returned home much the worse for liquor and assaulted her. Several times he had pulled her out of bed, pinched her, and pushed her against the wall. On one occasien, after pulling her from the bed, he overturned a lamp and set the room on fire. The complainant left hint and sought refuge in a neighbour's house. Defendant was fined LW and the costs, the magistrates also granting a separation to his wife, and ordering the defendant to pay ss. a week towards her maintenance.—Martha Aston, an elderly woman, of Prod- , sham, was charged with damaging some flowers belonging to Ralph Bazely, and also with assaulting Mary Brierly. On the 28th of June Bazeley's child was being buried. The funeral procession, on the way to the Parish Church, made its way across a field, and in this field the defendant came up and motioned the leaders to stop. The father of the deceased urged them to go on and take no notice of her. This they continued to do, when the woman, making a grab at the coffin, tore off the pall and threw away the flowers. Mary Brierly remonstrated a ith her, and she assaulted her. She afterwards walked away. The defence was that the field Was private property, and the funeral party were trespassers. Mr. Linaker, whop defended, contended that the magistrates bad no jurisdiction, as the question of right was raised. The bench took this view, and the cases were not further pro- ceeded with.

CONGREGATIONALISM IN LANCABIIIRE.-Tho Latina- shire .Congregational Calendar, 1881-2, just published, con- tains much that will be valued by those who are interested in the Independent churches of the county. The report of the Union, and the papers and addresses read at the annual meeting at St. Helens, in March last, deal with the problem " How to secure an increased attendance of the working classes at places of worship," and other questions of moment.l Particulars are given of the administration of the denomi- national societies and trusts, and of the progress of Conre- gationalism in various districts. The number of Congrsz'a- tional places of worship included in the Lancashire Union is 289, havingaltogether 151,051 sittings. It will be seen from the following statement that nearly one-half are in this part of the county :—Blackburn district has 53 churches, 25,792 sittings; Liverpool, 67 churches, 36.164 sittings; Manchester, 134 churches, 75.915 sittings; Pres- ton, 35 churches, 13,180 sittings. " Religious Statistics " are also given of eight towns in South Lancashire, showing the extent of the accommodation provided by the Church of England and other religious denominations. There is also the report of a sub-committee on the condition of the Lancashire Congregational churches in relation to Spiritual Life.

DARESBURY ERT-ry SEsstotss.—At these sessions, on Tuesday, before Mr. Edward Greensll and Mr. James Mar- son, Thomas Grice was fined 2s. 6d. and costs, for being asleep on his dray at Moore, on the 25th June.—For refus- ing to quit the Cat and Lion public-house, at Stretton, on the 18th June, two young men named Charles Russell and James Smith were each fined 58. and 10s. 6d. costs.—A boy named Peter Cartwright was charged with cruelly ill-treating and torturing a goat belonging to Mr. Woods. Defendant did not appear, and he was ordered to pay the costs.— George Norman was summoned for having on the Bth of July, at Whitley, made use of abusive language towards Alfred Barber. Mr. Slater appeared for the cornplsioant, and Mr. Moore for the defendant. Mr. Slater said this was a personal quarrel between farmers. Mr. Barber was a farmer at Whitley ; the defendant was a small farmer, and was also bailiff to Mrs. Massey, who employed Irishmen. The men quarrelled and rendered themselves extremely obnoxious to Mrs. Smith and Mr. Bitter. The unpleasant- ness culminated in a personal attack on his client's farm, several Irishmen running about and doing a great deal of damage. On the day in que,tion, the complainant was standing in his own g trden, when the defendant, who was passing, shook his fist at Mr. Barber, and mule use of extremely vulgar language. The defendaFg gavo the com- plainant to understand that if he did not "clear out of the place" soon he would smash kis head, as well as make it " hot " for him in future. In answer to Mr. More, com- plainant admitted that he called the defendant a liar. The C ialrrnan: We think this case ought not to have been brought here. And if Mr. Norman will make an apology for his conduct, the case is at an end. Mr. Moore, on defendant's behalf, did so, and the parties left the court.

Sin J. A. PICTON, KNIGHT. —Mr. J. A. Pioton, the chairman of the Liverpool Library, Arts, and Museum Committee, has been offered the honour of Knighthood by Her Gracious Majesty the Queen, and has accepted the same. The honour was one entirely unsought or expected by Mr. Picton, and will therefore be all the more valued. Mr. Picton's name in connection with art and literature is more than a local one, and this recognition of his work in the promotion and advancement of both those walks must, under the circumstances be most pleasing, not only to Mr. Picton, but to his constituents and friends, whilst even his political opponents, who have denied him civic honours, admit his ' claim to the distinction now conferred upon him by his Queen. It will be remembered that ha October, 1879, Mr. Picton was entertained to a public banquet at St. George's Hall, on the occasion of the opening of the Picton Reading- room. The banquet was the spontaneous outcome of the wishes of the leading people in Liverpool to give a public expression to the high position in which Mr. Picton stands in their estimation, and was attended as numerously by those opposed to Mr. Picton in politics, as by those with whom he had all along consistently acted. The chair wee taken by the Earl of Derby, and the company included nearly all the members of the Council as well as the leading citizens of Liverpool. Mr. James Allatnson Picton was born December 2nd., 1805, At that time the population of Liver- pool was not more than a tenth of what it is at present, and time has strangely altered many of its localities, notably Leeds-street, where Mr. Picton's father carried on the busi- ness of a timber merchant, and resided, as was the custom then, where he gained his bread. The father came to Liver- pool from Warrington, in which town, or in the neighbour- hood, several preceding generations kid lived. According to tradition, they were all men noted for some sort of clever- ness. They had amongst them almost all gifts except that of getting on in the world, which it seems they never did,
la. THI MA. BEASLEY'S BANKRUPTCY.

Mr. Beasley, solicitor, of Runcorn, and Widnes, and late clerk to the Widres Local Board, came up at the Liverpool Bankruptcy Court, yesterday, before Mr. J. F. Collier, judge, to pass his public examination. Mr. Segar (in- structed by Mr. Hitchen, solicitor, Runcorn,) appeared for several creditors, including Messrs. F. McDougall, Samuel White, James McQuinn, John Williams, and Joseph Richardson.

Mr. Bolland, the trustee, said that the bankrupt had not supplied him with the supplementary account which he agreeo to prepare, and he did not see how the case could be proceeded with under these circumstances. Mr. Seger said he was instructed to oppose the adjourn- ment, as he was quite prepared to carry on the examination that dey. They had now met three times for the purpose of examining Mr. Beasley, but an opportunity of doing so had not yet been offered. On the first occasion when the bankrupt ought to have appeared, and an adjournment was ,ranted, Mr. Beasley was acting as an election clerk at Frodsham ! He would consent to an adjournmont if the bankrupt would pay the costs which the creditors ,had been put to. If the supplemental account would render it unnecessary to examine Mr. Beasley, well and good; but he (the speaker) had not seen the account. Mr. Bolland again remarked that there was no supple- mental account, as vet. The bankrupt was preparing sue, and he, as trustee, should investigate it. Mr. Segar said it seemed to him that if the supplemental account covered the same ground on which he was going to examine the debtor, some portion of thejexamination might be unnecessary. However, if an adjournnsent was granted, the bankrupt ought to pay the costs. Mr. Bolland said there was no reason why Mr. Beasley should not be examined on that Occasion. Mr. Segar said he wished to examine the bankrupt upon one or two matters which he did not suppose would be in the supplementary account, and as to how much he held with reference to certain building transactions. After some further conversation, Mr. Seg sr consented to an adjournment being taken to the 12th August, on pay- ment of counsel's fees.

THE REV. J. GUTTEIDGE AT FRODSHAM.—A sermon was preached by the Rev. J. Guttridge. in the Methodist Free Church, on Wednesday afternoon, and in the evening the rev, gentleman delivered his deservedly popular lecture in the same place on " Christianity ; Its Divine and Human Side." The chair was taken by Mr. Samuel Wright, of Norley. The lecture was given with the usual ability of Mr. Gottridg,,, and it is to be regretted that th 3 audient, was so small. A collection was made at the close in aid of ' the funds for a minister's house which is in course of erec- tion in Church-street. ANNUAL TRIP OF THE FRODSHAM CHURCH CHOIR.-- The members of the Frodsharn ChurcWchoir had theirannual trip on Wednesday, the place vlected this year being Black- pool. The party, numbering 32, including the Vicar and the Rev. A. P. Reynolds, curate, left Frodsham station in a through carriage at 9-18 a.m., but in consequence of the northern train being half an hour late at Warrington, the company did not arrive at their destination until about one O'clock. This was an advantage than otherwise, as it enabled them to spend a pleasant hour in Preston. Os irrivilw at Blackpool the party amused themselves in various ways until half-past two, when all sat down to dinner. The different places of attraction were afterwards visited, including R tikes Hall Grr&ns, the Winter Gardens, the Aqu triton, the iron pier, dtc. The return journey was' commenced at 6-45. and all landed home safely, having spent a most enjoyable day. The weather was all that could be desired.

A WOMAN RUN OVER.-011 Tuesday evening an elderly woman named Hannah Forster, residing in Newtown, wav run over at Frodsham Bride by a conveyance belonging to Mr. William fiebbington, innkeeper. Frodsham Bridge, and seriously injured, one leg being broken and other parts of the body badly bruised.

TRELLT TO THE DUTTON WORKITOGSE CHILDREN.— t meeting of the Runcora Board of Guardians held on Tuesday, the Masterreported that on Fi iday the 22nd inst., Mrs. Hayes, of Frodsham gave the whole of the children an excellev. treat at her house, of tea, with bread, butter, hunloaf, and sandwiches. Various games were afterwards played 31) the grounds, and buns, oranges, and toys, were distributed on leaving. They all thoroughly enjoyed themselves, and the younger children were sent home in conveyances, the ho. :es being gaily decorated. A vote of thanks was unanimously accorded t • Mrs. Hayes for her kind and excellent treat.

div.head: CRIMINAL ASSAULT ON A NiARRIED WOMAN. SENTENCE ON THE PRISONERS.
div.p: THE CRIMINAL ASSAULT ON A NiARRIED WOMAN. SENTENCE ON THE PRISONERS.

Michael Devine and Peter Olohan, young men, were I indicted at Liverpool Assizes yesterday for assault. ing a rsarried woman named Margaret Havey.—Com- plainant, who is about 45 years of age, stated that ou a Saturday night, about ten o'clock, she called at a public-house in Newtown where she had 3 glass of beer, and she saw the prisoner Devine there. She left in a few minutes, and was walking to her home on the Old M irsh when she was overtaken by the prisoner Devine on the wooden bridge which crosses the railway. He threw her down, and ()Man having come up, he 'mid his hand over her mouth while Devine assaulted her.—P. C. Murray said that about ten o'clock on Saturday night, while on duty in Messrs. Gaskell and Deacsn's chemical works, he heard the suppressed screams of a woman coming from the direction of the wooden bridge. On going to the bridge he ow Devine and the other prisoner with the compl,inant. lic appre- hended Devine, who, after struggling and finding that he could not escape, admitted that he had assaulted com- plainant, and said he did not care if he got 20 years for it. Olohan was apprehended later in the evening.—The prisoners were each sentenced to ten years' penal servitude. .

div.head: MR. GLADSTON HEALTH.
div.p: MR. GLADSTON HEALTH.

In responding at the banquet to Mr. Gos.chen, on Wed- nesday night, to the toast of the Government, Sir W. Harcourt said :—I am sure, when speaking of the health of her Majesty's Ministers, there is one health which before all others is present to our minds, and that is the health of the man who is not only chief of the Administration of the , Queen, but is the foremost man of this age. (Loud cheers.) In responding to this toast, I am sure that there is present to your minds, as I am sure there is to mine, the health of Mr. Gladstone. (Cheers.) You share, I am sure, with those who sit around him, the unbounded admiration which he has inspired by his sublime ingenuity, by his indefati- gable patience, and by the indomitable energy which he has brought to the service of his country. At a time of life I when be has exceeded the allotted span of three score years and ten, he still, with undiminished force, with eyes un- dimmed, is at the service of his country, and this it is that makes him the pride of the Liberal party. (Cheers.) It is our pride and pleasure, to the utmost of our feeble abilities, to support him, and we feel that his unrivalled genius, his universal knowledge, and his matchless eloquence are beyond the hopes of our imitation. But still he sets to us all, in whatever station of life we may be, a lesson of un- selfishness and devotion to duty—(cheers)---and I confess that as we sit around him, and night after night sit beside him and contemplate the gigantic fortitude with which he sustains the Atlas load of the universe of care which he has to bear, I myself am filled with sentiments not less of fear than of admiration. We have toe few great men left among us gill. We can spare no more; and we cannot afford to oppress such men by the weight of superhuman toil. (Cheers.) I feel sometimes, especially in the weather from which we have recently suffered—(laughter)—that in that sort of malaria which oppresses and depresses the marshes of inediocrity—(laughter)---a something which revels in the contemplation of the higher landscape and the loftier out- lines of those elevated minds—there is something about it which makes one feel as if the fresh breezes blew on one from the summits of genius. lam happy to think that after this laborious session—and I took the liberty, while sitting beside Mr. Gladstone, to tell him—that he seemed ten years younger. (Laughter.) I think lam violating no private confidence when I repeat what he said to me when we were coming to the last clause of the Land Bill. Mr.. Gladstone said—., I look with some sort of childish satisfaction to the cheer which will be given when the chairman of committee leaves the chair." (Cheers.)

div.head: EDUCATION DRAG AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: THE EDUCATION DRAG AT WARRINGTON.

In our leading article last week, says The School l'oetrd Chronicle, upon the recent deputition to the Council office with reference to the paypent ef school fees by Boards of Guardians, we alluded briefly to the curious position taken up before the Lord President and Vice-pres dent by the representatives of the borough of Warrington in the deputa- tion. This week we report certain proceedings at a meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians, held since the inter- view at Whitehall, at which one of the representatives of Warrington, the Rev. Mr. Carleton, made a personal report of what took place at the Council office, and said some very strange things indeed on the national education question and on matters of detail as to the reception which the depu- tation met with. Mr. Carleton began by complaining that 1 Mr. Mundella did not treat with much ceremony the gentle- I men who appeared before him. The reverend gentleman waen he said tills, must have been thinking of the case ' sented on behalf of Warrington, and of Mr. Mundella's attitude towards tbe gentlemen who went from that borough , to Whiteli..ll, not so much to discuss the merits of the Tenth Section of the Act of 1876, as to make revelation to the autho.lties of Whitehall of the singular views entertained I ;ay ea many of the public men of Warrington as to the I establish.nent and the machinery of national education. We ' cannot sympathise with Mr. Carelton. We have watched 1 the doings of Warrington in this matter for some years, and the somewhat grotesque history of educa- tion in that town, from the date of the passing of Mr. Forster's Act until the present time, has not been unknown io the central authority. In 1870, when the first Act was passed, it was the misfortune of the general population of the town of Warrington to possess enough half-empty de- nominational schools to provide places for all the children in the borough, according to the census. We say it was a mis- fortune because the effect of the fact was to prevent the. Education Department from sending down a cotapulsory order for the election of a School Board. What was urgently wanted, all those years ago in Warrington, was a School Board to take proper measures for causing the chil- dren to attend school ; to take over by transfer any school that found itself unequal to the pressure of modern educa- tional demands, and to build a new school or two if it ap- peared that the existing accommodation was not suitable for certain classes of children requiring education. Unhappily the Act did not permit the Lords of the Committee of Council to issue an order for the election ef a Board, and it was the bad luck of Warrington to be represented, in its municipal character, by a Town Council entirely insensible to the spirit and demands of the age in educational matters. In every important borough in England where public feel- ing and local public men were awake to the progress of the Education question, and in sympathy with Parliament as to what ought to be done for the future welfare of the country, the Town Council, without waiting to ascertain whether the accommodation in denominational schools was suffi- cielt for the children; passed a resolution calling upoa the Lords of the Committee of Privy Council for an order for the election of a School Board; but the Warrington Town Council did nothing of the sort. It did nothing at all. The news, no doubt, had reached Warrington that Perlis- melt had spent the greater part of a Session in considering how to bring about the education of all the children in the country, and that an Act with that object had received the Royal sanction: but the will of Parliament and the Act of Mr. Forster had no effect whatever upon Warrington. The men in that town who boasted of their interest in education were contentio know that there were a certain number of Church schools, Roman Catholic schools, Wesleyan schools, and the like, and the question whether the schools were full or only half or one-third fell was apparently a matter of in- difference. At any rate, no attempt was made to introduce machinery fee causing the children outside the schools to be educated. And that state of things actually went on for six long years in Warrington—six years of tremendous moment in educational history, when the world was excited by the doings of the School Boards in London, in Birming- ham, in Manchester, in Liverpool, in every great town where there was any pretence of being abreast with the spirit of the time. What was the state of facts at Warring- ton during those six years of educational revolution in the land P Why, there were several thousands of children absent from school. There were two or three thousands who never saw the inside of a school. At a rough calculation we may say that durins, that six years some five or six thousand children passed from school age into adult age, ignorant and outcast so far as schooling is concerned, for no other reason than that the Town Council at Warring:on did not see fit to accept the School Board system. At last came the Act of 1876, which began to operate in 1877, and the Town Council appointed a School Attendance Committee. They took that step because it was forced upon them. The probability is that they would have gone on doing nothing, and flattering thernsel ,es on the existence of an abundance of denominational echool accom- modation, if there had been any mode of escape; but the appointment of attendance committees was imperative, and an attendance committee in the shape of a sub-committee of the Town Council was set up. These borough attendance committees have been important and useful bodies in some towns; but in Warrington the committee has been little more than a cypher. It has not been permitted to follow such prompting, towards efficiency as sprung up spon- taneously when the men were brought face to face with the Act of Parliament and the work before them. Everything they proposed to do involving expenditure was reviewed by the Town Council. debated at great length, and vetoed. It is not many months since the Town Council, with the fact before them that some two thousand children were habitually absent from school, refused to permit the attendarce com- mittee to appoint a second school attendance officer. And when, seeing how imperfectly the work of education in ac- cordance with the desire of Parliament was being performed in the borough a proposal was made at a Town Council meeting to adopt the School Board system, the motion was rejected by a very large msjority—the Aldermen and Town Councillors being, it seemed, of the opinion that the Town Council was a body of such commanding excellence that it would be better to amend the Education Acts so as to allow the Warrington Town Council to perform the functions wh*ch in ot, er boroughs are performed by School Boards. It was this last extraordinary theory that was propounded before Mr. Mon- della at the late interview, when, naturally without much ceremony in the face of a proposal so far-fetched and ab- surd, the right hon. gentleman inter...opted the speaker and saggested that the Warrington Town Council should pass a resolution requestinE the Education Department to issue an order for the election of a School Board. The Rev. Mr. Carleton went back to Warrington smarting uncle the insalt of this suggestion of the Vice-President, denouncing School %aids as unpopular, and proposing a resolution to the effect that the Town Council should constitute itself a School Board, whether such a scheme were level or not. As we have heard once again from Mr. Carleton, so we have heard from time to time durin,r, several years from aldermen, councillors, clergymen and guardians of Warrington, that the School Board is an unpopular institution. That is an unaccountable Warrington delusion. We know something about the history of School Boards, and we know nothing of their unpopularity—outside the borough of Warr;ngton and another place or two in that region. Another piece of in- formation afforded by Mr. Carleton is that School Boards are not on the increase, but' in places where they have been tried they have been given up. This is not in accordance with anything that we are acquainted with in the history of School Boards. Our annals go to show that they are in- creasing every day, and that no School Board has been g: /en up since the election ef the present Parliament. Mr. Carleton was, no doubt, thinking of Stockport, where the Slhool Board was dissolved by means of a deno&national and reactionary intrigue. Happily there is only one Stock- port, and it does not warrant Mr. Carleton's startling generalisation.

Mabel Wilberforce, aged 27, and described as Of no occu- pation, was brought up at the Westminster Police Court, yesterday, on a warrant by Inspector Robson, charged with having committed wilful and corrupt perjury on the sth inst. and four following days, in the Queen's Bench Division, in the remarkable libel case Wilberforce v. Philip. The prosecution was undertaken by the Treasury at the instiga- tion of the Public Prosecutor. Mr. St. John Wontner prose- cuted, and briefly opened the case. The prisoner was not represented, and some formal evidence having been taken the case was remanded.

E The charge against Mr. William Mair, the Liberal election agent at the last election for Macclesfield, was proceeded with at the Chester Assizes, on Thurs- day, before Lord Justice Baggallay. The evidence as to bribery was similar to that given in the previous case, and the result was the wame—namely, a verdict of guilty against the defendant, with a recommendation to mercy. Mr. Mair, like Mr. May, the Conservative agent, entered into recognisances to appear before the Queen's Bench for judgment.

THE BRADLAVGH MEETING.-Sir W. HARCOURT said he had seen the bill convening the Bradlaugh meeting in Trafalgar-equare for Tuesday. It did not propose that the meeting should do anythin4 prohibited by statute, and no intention was expleesed of proceeding to the House of Commons. He had received a copy of the instructions fromished to the leaders of the meeting, and perfect order was to be strictly maintained. There was, therefore, no legal authority upon which he could interfere. Every precaution would be taken to keep access to the House of Commons open.

AFGHANI/3T. AN.—The Marquis of HARTINGTON said the only additional telegram he had was received last night. It stated that two sirdars arrived from the scene of action. One of the Ameer's regiments deserted, and the other three fled. Firing was heard in the direction of Candahar. The loss is estimated at between 300 and 400 on both sides. General Hume was at Quetta with a force of 6.000 men. He was not aware of any fresh disturbance.—Sir W. BAJITELLOT asked if the Ameer had made a request for assistance to the Indian Government.—Lord HARTINGTON said he had no further information than that communicated. Until farther information was received from the Viceroy, it was not intended to take further steps. THE 'Rom LAN)) BILL —On the motion made .for, the third reading of the Irish Land Bill, Mr. W. H. SMITE moved the recommittal of the Mr. GLADSTONE objected to the recommittal of the Bill its it would not meet the objects intended. The motion for re- committal was negatived.—Lord B. CHURCHILL said the forms of the House prevented him now moving his motion, but he protested agiinst the passing of the Bill. He con- demned it as the outcome of revolutionary agitation.—Mr. G. Ittssxxx. vigorously retorted on Lord Churchill, and urged Mr. Gladstone to pass the speech with silence. —On . the question for the third reading being put, Mr. Gr-trisroxE expressed satisfaction that the leaders of the Opposition had not followed the example of Lord Churchill. He thanked those who had supported the Bill, and as regarded the attacks of the noble lord, there were smtll animals in creation whose office was to bite and irritate the blood, there were other small animals who bite without producing consciousness on the part of the victim that he had been bitten, and he was bound to say the noble lord reminded him of the latter. With regard to the Bill, he thought that required so defence.—Mr. GIBSON criticised the speeches of Mr. Gladstone delivered daring the progress of the Bill.— [r.acrr SITTING.]

A HALF Yitaa's ENORMOUS IMMIORLTION.—When the tide of immigration suddenly rose last year to a point beyond anything previously known, it was generally believed by those most competent to judge that the flood was due to ex- ceptional causes and would soon subside. But instead of falling it has continued to rise steadily and rapidly through ' every month of the present year. The a, rivals at this port during the half year just closed reacb,d the enormous num- ber of two hundred and forty thousand, which is about sixty-five thousand more than were landed during the first six months of 1880. The volume of immieration is always greater during the second half of the year. But unless there shall be an unexpected falling off during the comiLg moaths the arrivals at this port for the year will doubtless run up to four hundred and twenty or twenty- five thousand, or about one hundred thousand more than the great total of UM. As the number landed at New York represents about three-fourths of all that come to the United States, the aggregate immigration of the current year is likely to go considerably beyond half a million, a number that :would have been considered altogether improbable a few years ago. The chief cause of this steadily 'increasing irmnigration is unquestionably the general. prosperity that reigns throughout the country. The tide will doubtless fluctuate considerably in coming years, but there can now be little doubt that the number of foreigners added to our population between 1880 and 1890 will be far greater than . that known in any previous census decade.—New York Herald.

CRICKET. Sir —I have attended most of the principal matches that have been played on the Arpley cricket ground, and am glad to see a great iroprovemeit in the play of our town's club; but what surprises roe is that they do not let the professional play in matches, as I thick they have got a good cricketer in Denton, and most other clubs play theirs: and at the same time it would induce more people to come down to see the matches. Hoping the committee will consider the same, I remain, yours respectfully, A LOVER OF GOOD CRICKET.

div.p: THE WARRINGTON WATERWORKS AND THEIR

-- • • -----.__ RATES. Sir,—l am rather surprised no combined action seems to be in preparation to meet the next demand of the Water- *Ms Company. There can be no doubt that they will not let the present decision rest unless the public forget the clear Wording of the judge, and unless some concerted action is arranged they may be powerful enough to beat single-banded every individual ratepayer. It is surely the interest of every- body texcept the shareholders) to see that they PaY no more than can be avoided for the water sapply. There is no doubt that we pay enough, even taking the asses-ment instead of the gross rental, for it is not to be denied that six per cent. en the assessment is a very high percentage for a company having the exclusive privileges that our Waterworks Com- pany has. Let us be on the alert, and not find some morn- ing that they have got a decision in their favour. Here is an opportunity for our newly fledged Ratepayers' Associa- down the rates they tell us, and Hon. Their object is to teep surely this comes as much within the range of rates as either the poor or improvement rate. Don't you think that some action ought to be taken with respect to the past? The company ean be compelled to allow their accounts to be audited by an auditor appointed by the Court of Quarter Sessions, and if such an auditor were appointed we could soon get to know how much they had improperly taken within the last six years from the ratepayers, and then would it not awaken them if they hacrto disgorge? I do hope the matter may not be allowed to sleep' but that if the Ratepayers' Association do not move, some public spirited man will come forward, either in the Council or out, and set the ball in motion.—Yours. &c., CONSUMER.

DEAN STANLEY'S FUNERAL. A London correspondent writes :—Of all the funeral cere- monies wh:ch hive been performed in the Abbey, that of the Dean of Westminster was the most affecting within human recollection. Probably there never Lefore was such a widely representative gathering brought to a grave side by love and admiration. The Queen's representative was there, and flowers froia her hand lay upon the coffin. The Prince of Wales was there in person, and was accompanied by two of his brothers and see of his sisteis, the Princess Christian. Both political parties had their chiefs around the tomb. Mr. Gladstone and Sir Stafford Northcote, the Lord Chancellor, Lord Salisbury, and the Duke of Argyll, Lord Sherbrooke, Sir William Harcourt, and Mr. Smith m ngled their regrets together. But what would have pleased Dean Stanley more had he foreseen it, was the unity of men of all religions and none around him. With the Archbishop of Canterbury were half a dos m btshops of the Church; side by side stood the champions of orthodox Dissent, and the professors of the, newest Unitarianism. In one place was Dr. Allen, in an- other Mr. Stopford Brooke. The eye fell here upon the familiar face of a French Protestant, and there upon the strange fi4ure of an American priest, and tha leader of the Evangelical party, which was long Dean Stanley's bitterest fee. Lord shaftsbury came to pay tribute to the Christian character so lcng unjustly assailed. The only Quaker judge we have stood amidst the represmtatives of a proud prelacy. Nor were the scientific and advanced thinkers of the com- munity absent. Mr. Herbert Spencer was otherwise en- gaged, but Professor Huxley and Professor Tyndall, Mr. Leslie Stephen, Dr. Carpenter, Mr Leehy, and Mr. Froude were present. Nothing more touching than this scene of unity around the deaa has been seen even in the abbey. The service also was remarkable—musical but simple. There was grandeur in the solemn anthem, which reminded the con- gregation that a prince and a great man had fallen; but more pathos seemed to come from the final Nang in the nave Handel's rendering of the text" His body is buried in peace, but his name liveth evermore." At its conclusion, the vast congregation was melted to tears. It was vast; every niche of the abbey was occupied; every corner filled; and look in what direction one would, the same distinguished forms were to be seen. The impression made by the sight will never be effaced, and it is such a testimony to the great goodness of Dean Stanley, and the success of his teaching as the Apostle of Amity—as the French Protestants call him on ' their wreath—that his best friends would have not eaceaded by the highest hopes. The remains of the Dean of Westminster, were on Monday interred in Henry VIII.'s Chapel, Westminster Abbey. The funeral was fixed at four o'clock, but from about noon crowds began to assemble at the different doorways of the Abbey, a large number of those present being dressed in mourning. The entrances to the building were, however, closed to the public, it not being intended to open them until three o'clock. A large number of wreaths and mosses of beautiful flowers arrived at the Deanery, many of them accompanied by messages expressive of sympathy and regret. The Prince and Prime' of %VIPs sent wreaths, as did also other members of the Royal Family. As the pro- cession entered the. Abbey, through the west door the organist played Handel's anthem, "I know that my Redeemer liveth." After the choir, canons, and minor canons came the Archbishop of Canterbury, and then the coffin, which was of 'polished oak with brass fittings, and bore the following inscription :—"The Very Rev. Arthur Penrhyn Stanley. D.D., second son of the Right Rev. Edward Stanley, Bishop of Norwich; born 13th Decren.a' 1815; died 18th July, 1881." At the head of the coffin were placed the insignia of deceased's Order of the Bath, and on, tha 11l was a wreath of China roses with the ' wards' in Her Majesty's ' Own handwriting, "A. mark of sincere affection and high esteem from Victoria IL" Tlpi pall-bearers were Mr. Mattlreti'Arnold;the' Rev. Stbughtom'Carton Westcott, the Right Hon. W. 11. SMith, the Bishop of Exeter, Mt, Spottiswoode, the Rev. Dr. Storey (Master of Balliol), Mr. Forster, and the Duke of West- minster. Among the mourners were Lord Thurlow, re- presenting *the ileeen ; the Prince of Wales, the Duke of Connaugh4Prince Christian, the Duke of Argyll, the Duke of Richmehd„ Lord Shaftesbury, Lord Salisbury, Lord Derby, Lord Sherbrooke Mr. W. E. Gladstone, Sir Stafford North- cote, Sir Bartle irere, and Professor Huxley. Preceding the general procession of mourners were the relatives of the de. ceased—Dr. Vaughan. Lord and Lady Stanley, of Aiderley, the Dowager Lads, Stanley, Mr. and Mrs..Lvulph Stanley, Lord and Lady 'Elgin, Lord and Lady Airlie, the Bishop Suffragan of Dover, Mr. and Mrs. Locker, and Mr. and Mrs. Lionel Tennyson.
