Lome AND Factra.—fiteinthall's masterly summary of hese speculations on the "Origin of Language" is quite melancholy reading. It may, indeed, be brought forward as evidence to prove something that matters far more to us than the early history of language, that it is of as little use to he a good reasoner when there are no facts to reason upon as it is to be a good bricklayer when there are no bricks to build with.—Tylor's Early History of Mankind. Tim Bee-Caxt.--It had long been known that the bee- cell possessed the maximum of capacity with the minimum of material, and the cells being placed in double tiers, it was also found that their ends terminated in three diamond. shaped plates uniting in a point which exactly coincided with the centre of the opposite cell, so that each cell gave support to all those surrounding it, and was supported by them in Like proportion. That the mystery of the cell lay in the angler of these plates had long been suspected, and accordingly they were carefully measured, the measure- ments proving identical, no Matter who was the observer. Then calculations were made to solve problematically the question as to the form of a vessel which poesessed the maximum of capacity with the minimum of material,' and it was found theoretically to agree, with almost abso- lute exactness, with the bee-eelk'llatinwillita n therefore accepted the solution as "neat enough for all practical purposes," and so the question remained for a period of years. Bet, though naturalists might be satisfied, math& matieiana could not accept the "almost," and the problem was repeatedly investigated and always with the same result, namely, the persistent appearance of the obnoxious "almost." At last a Scotch mathematician named Mac- laurin bethought himself of investigating the mathematical table as well as the bee-cell, and found that in those tables by which astronomers had calculated the courses of the heavenly bodies, and the navigators directed the track of their ships, there was a mistake of a single figure. This single error was sufficient to invalidate all preceding astro- nomical predictions, and to wreck the vessels that were guided by them. So here we are brought face to face with the fact that the Creator knows no distinction between small and great. Roberts, B. B. Prescott, and E. C. E. Carleton; Messrs. Derbyshire, Winstanley, Greenall, Kilshall, Woolfall, Greening, R. Owen, Humphreys, Cartwright, Cooper, Garnett, Gibson, Heaton, J. C. The CLERK, adverting to the discuesien which took place , at the previous meeting of the Board in reference to the above subject, said the accounts were now certified by Mr. Mackey and himself, and as he did not think the difficulty would mite again, he, with the Board's approval, proposed not to subrnitthe matter to the Local Government Board, as had been previously decided Mr. DARBYSHIRE: I don't think you can take that course, Mr. Clerk, unless the proposer and seconder of the resolution are present and give permission. The CLERK explained that the bills were simply memo- randa, and did not come before the auditor. i Bev. J. YONGE said he was the one who moved the reso- lution, and did so because they were in such a glorious muddle. The Clerk was not present at the last meeting, but Mr. Samuel Sutton did the best he could to advise them. The Board weregoing into what seemed to him to' be an in- terminable discussion, and as no ene appeared to be able to throw any light on the subject, he moved that the matter be referred in the Local Government Board. As, however, Mr. Sutton had returned, and had been able to solve the matter, he submitted that the common sense course to take would be to strike out the resolution that had been passed. After a brief conversation, the considere'ion of the matter was deferred. THE WORKHOUSE' BAND IN REQtrEST. Rev. J. Thalia said Mr. Mackey had handed him a letter from the Rev. Canon Dodd, of Stretton. It stated that the school treat had been fixed for Friday, the sth Angust, and he should be glad for the band to be present. The goat of conveyance and a subscription to the band fund would be paid as usual. He (Mr. Yonge) moved that the necessary permission be granted. ' Mr. COOPER seconded the motion. Mr. WINSTANLEY, while not objecting to the motion, hoped the Board would take it seriously into consideration as to whether it would not be better to prohibit the band going out at all. Their going out interfered with the dis- cipline of the school, and did harm in other ways. Mr. WOOLFALL thought the Guardians should not make any exception this year. Mr. DAPBYSIIIRE remarked that an application of a similar character to the present bad frequently been refused by the Board on the ground that it came firma outside the Union Schools within the Union had always been granted the ser- vices of the band when the Board had thought it desirable, without much opposition or discussion. Stretton, however, was In another Union, and if the Guardians allowed the band to go be was afraid they would have a difficulty in drawing the the. Mr. COOPER: You forget they went to Southport. Mr. DARBYSHIRE: But it was for the benefit of some of the ratepayers who live in the Uni an. Major Caterwaionr observed that when the band went out other officials besides the bandmaster were taken from their duties. The CHAIRMAN did not think in the future any person would be allowed to go out with the hand except the band- master. The subject theta dropped, and the application was granted. THE ATTENDANCE OF OFFICIALS AT TEN MEETINGS.—LIVELY DISCUSSION. Mr. WINSTANLEY said that some time ago the Board passed a resolution that the Master should not remain in the room during the transaction of the special business; and he beg- ged to move "That it is inexpedient that either Mr. Mackey or Mr. Mines attend in this room during special business, but that they be requested to be in attendance outside to answer any questions that may be put to them." It was exceedingly unpleasant to a member of the Board to have the Master saying " Yes ; thank you, Sir." It was exceed- ingly unpleasant and very improper, and he hoped the Guardians would pass a resolution similar to the one that was passed before. Mr. WOOLFALL: Mr. Winstanley, will N al be kind enough to enlarge your resolution, and say that no person shall be allowed in the room except the Guardians and the clerk? (Laughter.) M. I dare say he would put in the reporters also. I did not know that there was anything private. Mr. WINSTASILEY (interrupting): No; he is not as fond of darkness as some people are. (Laughter.) It may be that the gentleman who has moved this re- solution, who has scarcely ever missed an opportunity, I may say, of "coming down upon" the Master of this house, any where where he thought be had power and the Master had no right to reply— Mr. GARNETT: That is a very improper remark to make, especiallve9 the Master is present. R, be had id before, m the !I-14(er as a Beard of Guardians they had DO right tOgiec:any opinion (in a mat. ter which pertained alone to the ratepayers of Warringhn. Of course if they in their individual capacity liked to give an

opinion to the ratepayers of Warrington, they might do so, but he maintained that it gave altogether a false impression and created a false opinion when that Board had to give a vote on a question which pertained solely to the internal. affairs of the town. He was surprised that Mr. Garnett seconded the motion. Mr. GARNETT: You would not have had an opportunity 'of speaking if I had not done so. (Laughter.) Rev. J. YONGE remarked that that was quite true. He I moved the following amendment: "That this Board declines Ito pronounce any opinion on the question of a School Board for Warrington, as it is a matter entirely beyond its jurisdiction." He thought that was a proper amendment to Mr. Carleton's resolution, and he hoped that members of the Board, and the country Guardians particularly, would feel that it was an amendment for which they ought to vote. A great deal, of course, could be said in answer to evnything Mr. Carleton had said that morning. He had made a great deal about the cost of School Boards, for in- stance. He (Mr, Yonge) could not help thinking it would do Mr. Carleton good if he would read the able speech Councillor Milner delivered in March, 1880, in regard to the formation of a School Board. Everyone knew that he was a man of calm temperament and great knowledge, and the speeches which he gave were most able, and, he thought, largely' unanswerable. In fact, it was amusing to notice the discussion which followed Mr. Milner's speeches. The speeches were simply expressions of opinion by the members of the Town Council why there should not be a School Board, and the majority of them were based upon the religious difficulty. In regard to the School Board Mr. Milner says "I believe that, to b ,gin with, all that a school board in Warrington would have to do would be to provide for about 500 children, either by means of an in- dustrial school or in some other way as more careful inves- tigation of the town might show to be desirable. You would require two school attendance officers to superintend the children. One in a town like this is of no use. You would want a clerk, and there would be certain office ex- penses which I put down at £3OO a year. * * * Sup- posing a new school had to be built for 500 children it would cost about £5 per head, or a total of £2,500. To borrow money in the ordinary way, which no doubt they would do at 6 per cent., with 30 years to pay it in, would give £3OO more, making the total of £6OO dead expenses for 30 years at ary rate. The cost of carrying on schools for 500 children would be £750 a year. A, against that £750 you would be likely to obtain in the first year about 12s. a head for the children in Government grant. Taking it at the present rate, that would give you £3OO. The children's pence would be about £lOO, and therefore the Board would have to contribute £350. making a total of £750. That £350 with the previous £6OO gives £950 as the expenditure of the Board to commence with, and a rate of 213. in the £ would give £1,082 ss. There is no need for a school board to cost more than that." Mr. Milner made that able calcu- lation with some knowledge of the whole facts. But he was surprised and amused at the way in which Mr. Carleton spoke in defence of our rich men. He said in a speech delivered a fortnight ago, if a school board were formed and a school rate laid our rich men would then have no channel for their generosity to flow in. (Laughter.) Surely they had not reached that state of almost millennial blessedness in this town in which the only one thing left to be supplied was the education of the children. He wished it were so. But he thought Mr. Carleton would known that although certain gentlemen were now very generous indeed in an educational direction, although that channel might be closed, there were thousands of other channels ready to be opened at any moment. Mr. Carleton said if they had not this channel of education to give their money in they would be obliged to confine their exertions to political agitation. That would be a most serious thing. But although he disliked it as much as Mr. Carleton did, he like a little dispute as much as he did. He thought in the immense amount of misery there was to be relieved on every hand our rich men would find a channel for their generosity, and, moreover, he might perhaps be allowed to say that men who were rich and generous might find an opportunity of giving to the Dis- senters. He did not think there was any risk to fear that our generous men would have their impulses for doing good stopped in any way. He was pleased to think that the time I was not far distant, whether they liked it or no, when a School Board in Wairington would be a fact; and he con- fessed he hoped he might live to see the time, and that it I would not be very long. Mr. GREENING seconded the amen'dment. Mr. R. OvrEN, in supporting the amendment, said there was nothing more beneficial than a School Board, and the School Board at Croft, which was one of the first in this district, had worked economically and thoroughly satisfac- tory to every inhabitant in the township. Rev. E. C. E. CARLETON, on being appealed to, withdrew his motion, and the amendment having also been withdrawn, most of the members left the meeting. THE STATE. OF THE HOUSE.

div.head: RAINHILL FLOWER SHOW.
div.p: RAINHILL FLOWER SHOW.
The fourth annual exhibition of the Rainhill Floral and Horticultural Society took place, by kind permission of Mr.
G. Anderson, of Be-acons.field house, in -a field admirably
adapted for the purpose, situated on the top of the hill, on Saturday. Four years have elapsed since the society was inaugurated, and each successive year has seen a marked
improvement in the show, that of Saturday altogether

eclipsing its predecessors, both as to the number of entries and the quality and variety of the exhibits. Unfortunately the weather, on which the success of out-door amusements and gatherings so much depends, was very unpropitious, rain descending heavily, almost without intermission, the whole of the afternoon, which not only considerably interfered with the comfort and pleasure of those who did put in an appear- ance, but materially affected the takings at the gate, and spoiled what would otherwise have been a great and de- serving,success. Besides the vast attractions the exhibition itself offered, the committee tad provided various kinds of amusements for the enjoyment and benefit of visitors, 80 that, had the weather proved favourable, there is not the least doubt a large concourse of spectators would have been brought together. As it was the amount taken would barely suffice to clear off expenses. The show was held in a corn- I modious and picturesque marqaee, 140 feet long by 50 feet I broad, provided and erected by Mr. A. Howard, of Red Cross-street, Liverpool ; and in i the exhibits were arranged with mach taste and effect. Through the centre of the ten: there was a display of stove and greenhouse plants, in and out of flower, which did infinite credit to the exhibitors; while the cut flowers, fruit, and vege- tables were exhibited on temporary benches erected round the sides of the tent. The staging was carried out by Messrs. Gerald Rawlins, G. Anderson, Sharkey, Lucas, Hankinson, and Rudge, and as there was no overcrowding :is on the last occasion, the exhibits could be seen to great ad- vantage. It would be alike difficult and invidious to par- ticularise, or descant on, the respective merits of the different varieties ot plants shown, but mention may Os made of the fuchsias, geraniums, petunias, gloxinias, and colenses, all of which were exceedingly fine, and bespoke much care and attention on the part of the gardeners of the gentlemen who owned them. The collections of 20 plants, in or out of flower, staged for effect, were grand, the premier prize' being secured by a Rainhill gentleman, while the se- cond was awarded to a resident gentleman of Iluyton who carried off the palm for six stove plants. There was a very nice show of cut roses, the special prize for the beat box of eighteen being borne off by a Prescot grower, who, though not a practical gardener, has taken great interest in the cul- tivation of the rose for over 20 years. Of the fruit, grapes constituted a prominent portion, the majority of the bunches being noticeable for their uniformity of growth, clean and fresh appearance, and the good colour they presented. The vegetables, if anything, were above the average, but do not call for any special remark. The exhibits in the cottagers' classes furnished ample evidence that the culture of flowers, fruit, and vegetables had been attended to, with appreciable results, as far as the humble resources of this portion of the population would allow. Inside and opposite the entrance to the tent was placed a large collection of new and rare plants, ornamental and foliage, consisting of palms, crotons, dracm nas, Am., suitable for the decoration of tables, &c., exhibited (but not for competition) by Messrs. Robert P. Ker and Sons, Aigburth Nurseries, near Liverpool. Mr. Henry Middle- burst, of Manchester-street, Liverpool, also had some plants and gardening tools on view; and Messrs. Dixon and Co., Upton Nurseries, and 106, Eastgate-street, Chester, con- tributed several boxes of large and magnificent roses. In all there were 75 classes, 61 of which were open, the remain- der being confined to cottagers residing within a radius of two miles from Rainhill station. The entries in all the classes totalled 430, being nearly double the number of entries last year. The donors of prizes included Mr. G. Anderson, Rainhill, who gave the first prize for four fachsiaa; Mr. Stead, Bold, special prize for eighteen cat roses; Mr. T. Davies, Sutton Heath Pottery, special prize of three ornamental vases, worth 305., for 30 trusses cut bloom pelargonium ; Mr. H. IV. Collins, Rainhill, first prize for four dishes of fruit; Mr. Cowan, the Vineyard, Garston, first prize for basket of three bunches of grapes, black or white; Mr. Joseph Bramham, horticultural engineer, 104, Dale-street, Liverpool, first prize for collection of twelve varieties of vegetables; and Mr. .J. Mather, Rainhill, who offered a special prize for tope window plants. In class 29, thirty trusses of cut bloom pelargonium, for which a special prize was offered, there were no entries, consequently there was no competition. As already stated the attendance of visitors was not Sr large as usual, not more than 500 being' present at any portion of the day. During the afternoon the Prescot Victoria Quadrille Band played selections of dance music, the programme being as follows: —March, "The standard ;" fantasia, "Rose of love;" polka, "First rose;" quadrilles, "Alliance ;" waltz, "Loved and lost;" schottische, " Snowdrop ;" gallop, " Speedwell ;" fantasia, "Croix de Flonnenr ;" quadrille, "Wheel of fortune ;" waltz, " Snow wreath ;" polka, "Merry Elves," dm. Immediately opposite, and at a short , distance from the exhibition tent, was erected a temporary' I stage or platform, on the boards of which the celebrated American starr minstrels performed several comic pietas; the screaming sketch "Ginger, or Pop in trouble," and the sketch "School Board, 1381," attracting much attention and' lf exciting the risible faculties of the onlookers. At various I intervals, songs, overtures, choruses, flute, harp, and violin solos were also given. At one side of the field was a re- freshment tent, the caterer being Mr. A. C. Doe, of the Stanley Arms Hotel, Roby. It may be mentioned that the patrons of the society include, the Marchioness Stapleton Bretherton, the Marquis of Salisbury, the Earl of Derby, Lord Skelmersdale, and Mr. Rudolph Willis, of fialsnead. The president is the vicar of Rainhill, the Rev. J. Barton, who was present at the show on Saturday, and the list of vice-presidents, fifteen in number, comprises the names of some of the leading gentlemen in Rainhill and district. Thel arrangements for the show were carried out by a committee ' consisting of the following gentlemen :—Messrs.. J. Brother-] ton, T. Chesworth, H. Clifton, J. Early, H. Flowers, E. Goodwin, J. Hatton, A. Hankinson, W. Hopecroft, D. Lucas, J. Pratt, J. Mather, and T. Sharkey. The treasurer is Mr. H. W. Collins, of the Firs, Rainhill, and the secretary, Mr. J. Rudge,Victoria-terrace, Rainhill. To the latter gentle- man a word of praise is especially due, for the excellent manner in which he discharged the onerous duties of his office. The judges were Mr. Jamieson, Haigh Hall, Wigan; Mr. Mason, Prince's Park, Liverpool; and Mr. M. A. Cole, Didsbnry, Manchester. The following is a list of the awards:—

On Friday evening, a meeting of the ratepayers of the township of Whiston, was held in the National School-room for the" purpose of protesting against the appcintment of assistant overseer as made by the guardians, and petitioning the Local Government Board thereon."—Mr. WILLIAM GERRARD presided, and there were about 100 ratepayers present, including Mr. John Leatherbarrow (guardian), Mr. Henry Smith one of the overseers), Mr. 0. Ward, Mr. Jas. Blundell, M. Pennington, Mr. R. Storey, and Mr. D. Sed- don.—Phe CHAIRMAN, in opening the meeting, said a great deal of dissatisfaction was felt at the appointment of Mr. Edmund Range, of Prescot, as the assistant overseer for the township of Wbiston, and he thought for very good reasons. He d d not th nk the Guardians had any necessity to travel out of the township to find a man to do Whiston 's work. There were plenty of men in the town- ship quite competent and able enough to act ac assistant overseer. There were two or three c indidatee for the post freer Whiston, all of whom were equal to the gentleman who had been appointed. It was for the meeting to enter its protest egainst the manner in which Mr. Range had been appointed. There appeared to have been a good deal of underhand work in the appoint- ment, but he could not go so far as to say that it had been made illegally. There were candidates from Whiston, one of whom had a testimonial signed by a large number of influential ratepayers, in his favour, but he believed that testimonial was not read,—in fact, not even looked at. He thought that was an insult to the intelligence of the rate- payers of Whiston. Unfortunately their representative at the Board was not able to be present when the appointment was made owing to illness. Had he been there be (the chairman) felt confident things would have taken a different direction. (Hear, hear.) He thought their representative would not have allowed the matter to be scouted and over- ruled in the manner it was. It seemed that the ratepayers of Whiston were not to have a voice in the management of their own affairs at all. He was of opinion that the appointment of assistant-overseer ought to be made by persons residing in the township, and persons to whom he had to pay the money. They did not want to trust money in the hands of aux gentleman of whom they knew nothing about. They wanted a man they knew something of, and a man in whom they could place some reliance. If the Guardians had consulted and com- plied with the wishes of the ratepayers they would have elected one of the candidates from Whiston. (Applause.) —Mr. D. SEDDON asked if it would be any use to send a memorial to the Guardians to see if the resolution could be rescinded. He meant before the appointment was sent up to the Local Government Board for confirmation.—The CHAIRMAN replied that the appointment would very likely be retitled by the Local Government Board before that could be done. He thought a petition ought to be sent to the Local Government Board before that could be done. He thought a petition ought to be sent to the Local Govern- ment Board'at once, protesting against the appointment.—. Mr. SEDDON observed that it would be better if they could get the resolution rescinded before it was sent up for con- firmation. If there was not time then by all means petition the Government Board.—Mr. LEATHERBAIIROW (guardian) remarked that as far as the Guardians were concerned the appointment was already made. It only required the con- firmation of the Local Government Board. It would be useless to send the petition to the Board of Guardians, as they could not rescind their own action conscientiously.— Mr. G. WARD asked if the newly appointed collector had got a bond. If so, then it was quite right he should have a trial. It was a bit of bad grace to try and throw him out. —Mr. SEDDON remarked that perhaps Mr. Ward would bear in mind that it was not the wish of the ratepayers that an outsider should be appointed. The ratepayers wished to have the management of their own affairs.—Mr. WARD in- quired how it was that the Whiston men who applied for the post were thrown ont.—Mr. SEDDON : That is what we want to know, and that is what this meeting is called for. —Mr. WARD : It was left to the Guardians, arid they ap- pointed who they thought was the best inan.—Mr. UT. Salmi (an overseer) : Neither the overseers nor the rate- payers want him, nor will they have him.—Mr. J. STOREY remarked that the appointment did not meet with the approval of either the Guardian of the township or the ratepayers, and therefore he did not think it was a consistent one.—Mr. RUSHTON was of opinion that as the ratepayers of Whiston appointed their own Guardian, they should appoint their own assistant-overseer.—Mr. H. Szarrit : The ratepayers of Whiston have to pay the wages of the assistant-overseer, and ,why should we not be allowed to elect who we like.—Mr, Taos. SMITH : It seems strange to me that we can appoint our overseers and yet not the assistant-overseer.—Mr. SMITH: I should think so.—The CHAIRMAN said the question was, "Was the appointment in accordance with the wishes of the ratepayers ?" [Voices: Na.] The feeling of the meeting seemed to be emphatically against it. lie had not spoken to one ratepayer who did not feel dissatished with the manner in which the township bad been treated. Under the circumstances he thought the ratepayers were perfectly justified in holdings public meeting to protest against the appointment. He bad not the least doubt if thy I entered a protest and forwarded a petition signed by the ratepayers, to the Local Government Board, something would be done in the matter.—ln answer to a question, Mr, LEATHERRARROW stated that he forwarded the testimonial signed by the ratepayers in favour of Mr. Watkin to the Selection Committee in order that it should be read and con- sidered at that committee. He was very much surprised to 'mar from the Rev. T. Chambers, who called to see him on the Thursday, that the one whom they thought would have been elected had' been left out in the cold.—After some further cohversation a committee of five gentlemen was ap- pointed to draw up a memorial to the Local Government I Board, protesting sasainst the appointment. The memorial was as follows:--" We, the undersigned, ratepayers of the township of Whiston, in public meeting assembled, beg to enter our solemn protest against the appointment by the Guardians of the Prescot Union, at their inee;irig held on Thursday, the 14th July, of Edmund Range, as assistant overseer for the tow ',ship of Whiston. Our reasons for this protest are:—First, that there were appli- cants from the said township, and more in accordance with the wishes of the ratepayers generally, one of whom (Mr. Tames Watkin) had fulfilled the duties of assistant overseer of the township for upwards of two years, to the entire satie- faction of the overseers and ratepayers of the townsbip. secondly, we object en the ground that the memorial signed try ratepayers representing at least three-fourths of the rateable value of the township, presented in favour of Mr. James Watkin appeared not to have been taken into con- sideration by the Guardians. Thirdly, we consider that the appointment vas not made on the merits of the candidates for the office, nor is the appointment in accordance with the wishes of the overseers of the said toiviiship ; and further your petitioners are of opinion that the wishes of the over- seers and ratepayers ought to be consulted in the appoint- ment of assistant overseer of the township." It was-under- stood that the memorial would be taken round the township on the following morning to be signed by the ratepayers. A vote of thanks to the chairman concluded the proceedings.

PRESCOT BOA ID OF GUARDI A NS.
A LIVELY MEETING.

The usual fortnightly moetine of this Board WU held on Thursday, at Whiston Workhouse, Mr. S. Marsh, presiding. The other members present were—Revs. T. Chambers and J. Barnacle, Messrs. J. T. Hall. G. J. Faris, J. Fisher, W. A. Meadows, J. Ranson, W. Gerrard, J. Fidler, J. Lowe, Joseph Jackson, W. Gilbody, J. Matthews, T. Sadler, E. Syder, T. Retook, J. Leatherbarrow, T. Dobell, J. Kenwright, W. Tyrer, S. Rowe, and E. Birch; with Mr. S. H. Hartley, clerk.

THE WORKHOUSE MASTER'S REPORT. The Meer= reported that the number of inmates in the house at the end of the week was 491, against 495 in the preceding week. and 537 in the corresponding week of last year. There were 138 boys and girls at Kirkdale Schools. 173 vagrants relieved during the week. The larder at the hospital appeared to have been entered by thieves during Sunday night or early on Monday morning, and some groceries and cooked meat stolen. The bread pantry seemed to have been entered from the window at the same time. As a piece of uncooked meat was left untouched, and a key that fitted in the locks was left behind, it is probable that some person on the premises or familiar with the house is concerned in the matter. The Master asked to be allowed to get a few fresh locks on the doors, and some iron bars for the windows where necessary. Mr. Ottiwell, of Ilalsnead, offered to supply good wheat straw at 2s. 9d. per cwt., pro- vided be had the supply until Christmas.—lt was resolved that the Master be allowed to get the locks and bars for the doors and windows. The offer of Mr. Ward was refused. The Master having reported that the flour supplied to the Workhouse by the contractor was unsatisfactory, it was resolved that the same be returned.

THE WORKHOUSE ACCOMMODATION. At a meeting of the General Purposes Committee, Dr. Hall's report on the overcrowding in the Workhouse was read, and it was recommended that professional opinion be obtained as to the best means of increasing the accommoda- tion by utilizing and extending the present buildings, that the sum of ten guineas be allowed for the expenses of such opinion; and that the names of Messrs. Culshaw and Sumner be submitted to the Guardians to give the opinion referred to.—Recommended that butter be made in the Workhouse from milk supplied there; and that the clerk be empowered to take samples of the milk occasionally, and cause the same to be analysed by the public analyst.—The recommendation respecting the making of the butter was negatived by ten to six.—A long discussion ensued with regard to the Work- house accommodation, in the course of which it appeared that the question of overcrowding had been before the Board and the General Purposes Committee on two and on three occasions, and postponed.—ft was resolved, on the motion of Mr. FISHER, seconded by Mr. RANSON, that Mr. Sumner, architect, Liverpool, be asked to give his opinion as to the best means of providing further accommodation by extending the present buildings. OUTBREAK OF SMALLPDX AT ST. HELENS. The CLERK said he was sorry to report that smallpox had made its appearance in the borough of St. Helens, in the township of Sutton. He only heari at two o'clock on the previous day, and he telegraphed to Dr. Beard, the Local Government Board inspector, who, he hoped, would take some steps in the matter. The outbreak was tiutside the Prescot Rural Sanitary Authority's district.—Mr. MATTHEWS : There is also a case in Whines.

- _ THE COUNTY CALL.-CONSIDERABLE INCREASE. The CLEux produced a precept from the Clerk of the Peace requiring tbe payment on or before the 22nd day of August Of £7,618 Sc. sd. by the overseers of the different townships of the Union for county police and other charges. The amount of the call last year was £5,555 10s. id, showing an increase this year of £2,062 15s. 4d. The assessments on the townships are as follows :-Bold, £lBO 78. ; Oronton, £46 13s. Bd.; Ditton, £ll6l ; reclestw, £6ll 9s. 3d.; Hale, £56 Os. 7d; Halewood, £282 6s. 7d.; Huyton-with- Roby, £522 Os. 4d.; Knowsley,£lB9 128. 101 ; Parr, £385 On. 9d.; Present, £152 15s. 7d. ; Rainford, £277 78. 3d.; Rainhill, £206 Sc. 2d.; Speke, £l3O 118. 41; Sutton £1,377 18s. ad.; Tarbock, £72 78. 5d.; Whiston, £282 16s. Bd.; Widnes, £1,277 98. 6d.; Windle, £915 lie. 7d.; Little Wool- ton, £217 3s. 10d.; Much Woolton, £317 17s. 4d.-On the motion of Mr. Eavocx„ seconded by Mr. JACKSON, the pre- cept was ordered to be signed. APPOINTMENT OF MEDICAL OFFICER FOR HUTTON. The CLERK read an application for the office of medical officer and public vaccinator of Huyton district from Mr. Henry Gorst, of Oak Hill, Huyton.-Mr. PARIS moved that Mr. 'Gorst be elected to the office.-Rev. T. CHAMBERS seconded, and the motion was unanimously agreed to.

div.head: APPOINTMENT OP PORTER &ND PORTRESS.
div.p: APPOINTMENT OP PORTER &ND PORTRESS.

A special meeting of the Guardians was held on the 26th. inst. to consider the applications for the office of porter and portress at the workhouse. There were 35 applications, and four were selected to appear before the Guardians at their next meeting. It was resolved that John Scannell, who had been storekeeper at the Bolton workhouse for eighteen months, and his wife, be appointed to the office, at a salary of £35 per annum. , Mr. J. T. Harz, in accordance with notice of motion, pru- ' posed that the salaries of 'Mr. Parkinson, relieving officer, of Prescot, and Mr. Goff, relieving officer, of Widnes, be in- creased from £lOO to £l2O per anniim. Mr. Hall pointed out that twelve months ago the Board unanimously agreed that Mr. Parkinson should have an increase ef salary, but on the sanction of the Local Government Board being sought, the latter thought as Mr. Parkinson was a young officer the matter should stand over for a short time. He then quoted statistics showing that in other unions, with similar populations to Prescot, the relieving officers were getting considerably more than either Mr. Parkinson or Mr. Goff. It had been admitted that Messrs. Goff and Parkinson were two of the best officers they had, and therefore they should pty them in proportion to their ability and the work they did. When Mr. Goff was appointed he was distinctly told that the salary would be a progressive one, and he (Mr. Hall) could safely say that there had never been a complaint against him.—Mr. FIDLER seconded the proposition, and remarked that the two officers were very assiduous in their duties, and if they wanted to retain men of ability and char- acter, they must pay them properly.—The Rev. T. CHAMBERS endorsed the remarks of the previous speakers.—Mr. MEADows agreed that Messrs. Parkinson and Goff were goodl officers, but considering the state of trade in the union. he I did not think the present was the time to raise their salaries. He thought it would be better to defer the question for the present. —Mr. Marrnaws would like to know why Mr. Meadows was always on the one tune. He considered that the officers were fairly entitled to the increase.—After further discussion, it was resolved by large majorities that the officers' salaries should each be increased to £l2O per annum; and that the salary of Dr. McNicoll, medical officer, St. Helens, increased to £9O per annum. ALLEGED " SHELVING " OF A MEMORIAL: WARM DISCUSSION.

Mr. LEATHERBARROW said he was requested by the majority of the ratepayers of Whiston to express their re- gret and to enter their prctest that the memorial presented to the B ard (in favour of Mr. James Watkin) signed by the majority of them and bearing signatures of gentlemen re- presenting three-fourths of the rateable value ef the town- ship, received such slight consideration at the bands of the Board, iu the selection of assistant overseer for that town- ship.—The CHAIRMAN remarked that the selection bad been made, and therefore whatevei Mr. Leatherbarrow might say would have no effect.—Mr. LEATHERBARROW: I am aware of that. lam merely entering my protest.—The CHAIR- MAN: I know that, but I think it would have been better if you had made it at the time.—Mr. LEATHERBARROw : I was unfortunately, unable to be present at the meeting. I would not have brought the matter before you to-day, had not one of nay brother Guardians added insult to injury by producing a paper, which was handed over the table at the meeting, bearing the words, "If you will run Houghton for Crouton, we will support Range for Prescot," or something to that effect. If that is the way our outside officers are to be appointed, the sooner we throw up the ap- pointments the better, and let them be made by the Local Government Board.—The CHAIRMAN did not see anything wrong in it. Any one gentleman could say to another "If you will vote for my friend I will vote for yours."—Mr. HALL : Did you see any paper passed round P—The CHAIR- MAN: I don't think! did.—Mr. LEATHERBARROW : It was passed along in Whiston, and the remark was made, " This is the way we 'fluked ' you, because your man was not there."—Mr. FIDLER: It's most disgraceful.—Mr. DOBELL : Mr. Fidler may wink, but I think it's mostderogatory to the dignity of this Board.—Mr. FIDLER (rising hastily): I beg your pardon--. Mr. DOBELL: I saw you distinctly.—Mr. FIDLER (indignantly): I am no party to circulating the paper.—Rev. T. CHAMBERS questioned very much whether it was not the business of the Board to take notice of what Mr. Leatherbarrow was cognisant of with regard to the elec- tion of public officers of that Union. He differed from the view taken by the Chairman on the subject. He cer- tainly entered his protest against such work; and he blushed for the fair name and fame of the Guardians of the Prescot Union, if elections were carried on in that way.—The CHAIRMAN: Did you ever know elections carried on honestly and straightforwardly? If every man would only tell the truth from the commencement to the termination you would find that the greatest hypocrisy is carried on.—Rev. Mr. CHAMBERS: Than it is our duty as a Board to do as much as we can to stop it.—The CHAIRMAN: But we cannot stop it.—The Rev. T. CHAMBERS characterised it as all a farce and sham to insert advertisements in newspapers asking can- didates to offer themselves and to send testimonials and recommendations, if, when the Guardians met, they did not attend to them, but voted for a man irrespective of his testimonials. He entered a respectable protest against such practices in the Union.—Mr. HALL: Did you see any paper pass round.—Rev. T. CHAMBERS: No, but Mr. Leatherbarrow says he has been told it was passed round.—Mr. HALL said he was confident no paper passed round in that room.—Mr. FIDLER (to the Chairman): Mr. Dobell has addressed you with re- ference to my conduct in this room. If! did not know bow to conduct myself I should not go to Mr. Dobell to be taught, and I say that Mr. Dobell has no right to found an accusation against me upon the fact that I winked at Mr. Hall or Mr. Leatherbarrow.—The CHAIRMAN: Well, it does not matter.—Mr. FIDLER: I resent it as an insult.—The matter was then allowed to drop.
TIM EXA MINER, SATURDAY, JULY 30, 1881.

div.p: more easily managed than the girls, being really more in- telligent. Tho girls were tidy-looking; but Miss Whately quired if their parents had no scruple said she had great difficulty in bringing them into habits of cleanliness. We in about their being placed under Christian influences She said considerable prejudice had to be overcome at first, and, even now, she believed that, in most instances, the readiness to send the children arose out of pure ignorance, although they were fully informed 'of the object of the mission. She thought also, that the fruits, in better behaviour at home on the part of the girls, operate as strong inducements to send the children to school. The girls were learning Arabic and English, sewing snd embroidery. Miss W. mentioned the diffic thy she had to keep the girls until they were 14 years of acte ; the usual marrying age being 12, and not un- frequently 10, it was almost impossible to do any good with them after they reached the age of 12. M,EI9 Whitely has folds copya s ot hof ooh bke eer , t silkrhe ias d vml a da tnyot beganie,accom- pany t too now an Arab Bible woman under her direction. Whilst we wereafarrsateynlherself g hi neartthe heei7g ipgr iloes ' Miss Whately on her rounds to die Arab huts and homes. The native women who undertake this duty are very shy about entering the houses, and Miss W., with indefatigable energy, has to go along with them in the first instance. This most estimable and persevering lady thus enters in the fullest manner, into the spirit of the mission, and bends every power of her keen strong mind and vigorous frame to the accomplishment of its benign ends. She has laboured under all the difficulties and discourage- ments of her position for 15 years, and from what we saw, seems not to "bate one jot of heart or hope" in Labouring for its ultimate success. Her remark was, that, so far, it had I been rather a sowing time than a reaping time; but, from what I could learn, the fruits, in spreading over the Orient a class of men well-educated in English, and having a good knowledge of the Bible, are at this time very visible, and are contributing very greatly to the ease and comfort with which the English travel through the East. Some of the best dragomen have been trained in these English schools, scat- tered over Egypt and Palestine. (To be continued next week.)

ACCOUNTS. In addition to the cheques ordered for payment at the last meeting, the following had oeen passed :—Vaccination and registration, £6B (3. 6d.; extra medical fees, £5 175.; re- moval expenses, £3 7s. 81; loan account, £35 3s. 6d.; Union fund expenses, £56 18s. 6d ; total, £l2B 18s. 104.—Mr. HANDLEY observed that the expenditure was about equal to tnevious quarters. HOSPITAL EXTENSION. On the motion of Mr. HAELEHDRST, seconded by Mr. McitrrvitE, it was decided to advertise for tenders for the extension of the Hospital. TEE BASIS OF COUNTY RATING. The CLERK Said that in accordance With the resolution of the Board he had addressed a communication to the clerk of the peace for the county, asking that a revision of the county rates might be made. At the last Knutsford Ses- sions, the deputy clerk of the peace, laid the letter before the magistrates. He stated he had had some correspondence with Lord Egerton. of Teton, who desired him to say to the magistrates, what he said at the last Quarter Sessions at Knutsford, that the subject had not at all escaped his at- ention ; but there had been so many bills brought before Parliament for the valuation of property for reing purposes that he thought it was quite useless to go to the expense and trouble of revising the county rate ; for should one of these bills bDcorne law all the expense and trouble would be thrown away. Ills lordship, the, efore, did not think it a prudent time to make a re-valuation.—Mr. DARRYSTIIRE: There seems to be a little misunderstanding. —The CLERK I don't see bow they could misunderstand my letter.—Mr. HAZLERURST said it seemed to him that an independent valuation must be taken to be of any real service. Had an independent valuation been taken ? The CLERK said the basis was revised in 1873 ; a committee of magistrates were appointed at the Quarter Sessions, and they took into consideration the several returns front the uions in the county.—Mr. Ilmatnersterr : Then it was not an independent valuation 7—The CLERIC Said it Was not.— Mr. HaarbutY remarked that they bad a County Rate Com- mittee, and as they had stirred the matter up they ought to go on with it.—A MEMBER asked if they could not appeal against the next county rate.—The CLERK said it was legal to appeal against all county rates levied upon them. It was a serious question whether they ought not to appeal. There was no doubt they had not been treated properly.—Mr. NORMAN moved that the County Rite Committee be called together at some early day to consider what further action should be taken.—Mr. DARBYSITIRE seconded the motion, which was carried.

MONDAY.—Before Mr. George Pilkington. BEOGING.—Wm. Murphy was committed 14 days for being guilty of this offence in Victoria-road. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. Earle (chairman) and Mr. J. Bibby. A SOMEWHAT "Mix" CASE.—A case was heard in which four women were conceined. A Mrs. Ashley, James- street, was summoned for assaulting Mrs. Mullinger, and there was a cross-summons in which the last named woman was charged with assaulting Mrs. Ashley. A Mrs. Sutton was I keviise charged with an assault on Mrs. Ashley, for whom Mr. Swift, jun., St. Helens, appeared. On the day of the disturbance Mrs. Mullinger and some of the other women in the case had been to the St. Helens County Court, and on their return, as they were passing up one of the Widnes streets, Mrs. Mullinger said something to Mrs. Ashley about pawning some clothes. Mrs. Ashley threatened to hit her with a brush which she had in her hand, on which Mrs. Sutton interfered. The two parties afterwards had a regular fight. One of the witnesses stated that most of the women in the case had been to St. Helens County Court, and bad a plentiful supply of drink whilst is that town.—Mr. Swift, in defence, said that Mrs. Mullinger had been to St. Helens to drawn some money and get her dress out of pawn. Whilst there she had something to drink. On her return to Widnes she saw Mrs. Ashley, and twitted her about her (Mullinger's) dress not being in pawn. Mrs. Ashley told her she did not care anything about her dress, on which Mullinger struck her two or three times in the face. Mrs. Ashley afterwards hit Mullinger with a brush.—The summons against Ashley Was dismissed; and Mrs. Sutton and Mrs. Mullinger were each ordered to pay 10s. and costs 115. firl. DEFAMATORY LANGUAGE.—Thomas Young was ordered to be bound over in his own recognisances of £lO and one surety in £5, to keep the peace towards Ellen Hunt for one month, he having charged her with having stolen 2s from him.—Sarah Kenny was brought up on a warrant after sum- mons, for using similar language to Mary Ann Murphy on the 11th inst. The case having been proved the prisoner was ordered to find sureties as in the last case, or in default be sent to goal 14 days. DAMAGING GRASS.—A girl named Alice Hunt was fined is. and costs Sa. for doing damage amounting in value to 61. to growing grass belonging to William Thar.ne, on the 22nd inst. A VIRAGO.—Mary Tracey was summoned for assaulting Mary Welsh on the 22nd inst.—Complainant said defendant came to her house, used very bad language, and seized her by the hair.—Defendant, who pleaded guilty, was fined 20s and costs 78 6d, or in default of payment one month's im- prisonment. On hearing the sentence she began to tell the story of her wrongs, but she was told that the Bench could not enter into it then, as she had pleaded guilty. SYstaranct 114 Lass. OF litorr.—Alice Flood and Mary Bry- son were charged on remand with stealing 114Ibs. of iron, the property of the London and North-Western Railway Company.—Mr. Ferrand, from the solicitors' department, Lime-street, Liverpool, appeared to prosecute.—P.C. Strick- land said that on the previous Monday night, about a quer- ter-nast eleven at night, he was on duty in Warrington-road, Lugsdale, when be saw the two prisoners coming across a field from the direction of the London and North-Western railway. He followed them, as he noticed they were carrying something bulky, and on getting up to them he found them with the iron. The women said they did not think there was any harm in taking the iron, which they had got from a wagon near the Alkali Works.—Thomas Jackson, platelayer in the service of the company, gave evidence as to having missed iron from the works, but said this was some time since. Each of the prisoners was sentenced to 21 days' hard labour. Ax Usrmaxtmar. FATHER.—Patrick McMahon, who had been brought up on warrant, was charged with having left three of his children chargeable to the Presnot Union.—Mr. Gough, relieving officer in the Widnes district, said he had his attention called to the totally destitute condition of the prisoner's children by Mr. Dickson, nuisance inspector to the Local Board. He found them in a temporary lodging in which they had been placed prior to their removal to the Workhouse. Prisoner was a lazy fellow and would not work.—Mr. Dickson was called, and said that on the even- ing of the 27 instant he found two of the man's children wandering about the street, and, having known them for a long time, he asked them what they were doing. They told him that their father had deserted them, and the landlord of the house had turned them out because the rent h td not been paid. A woman took the children in, but they were so filthy that she refused to let them remain, and he had them re- moved to a lodging-house. Prisoner was idle, drunken, and worthless. Witness concluded his evidence by saying that on an occasion when one of prisoner's children died, he behaved in-a most callous, bard-hearted manner. Pointing to the coffin which some men had gone to the house to take away, he said "There's your load,—take it."—The Chair- man said the prisoner would be comrottted to gaol one month, with hard labour, unless he was able to make some arrangement with the relieving officer, which he said he was not prepared to do. STEALING LEAD.—A youth named William Bayliss was charged with stealing Bibs. of lead, the property of Messrs. Golding, Davis and Co., on the 21st instant—The Inspector of Police said that the prisoner was seen going out of the ' works, and, on being stopped by the watchman, the lead was found in his possession, and he was given into custody.— The Chairman said the prisoner would be fined 10s., and would also have to receive six strokes with the birchrod. CHARGE AGAINST THE INSPECTOR OF POLICE.—At the close of the proceedings—just before the magistrates had left the Bench—Mr. Bartlett, solicitor, Liverpool, said he had come to the court for the purpose of appearing in a Case in which Mr. Barnett, the inspector of police, was sum- moned for an assault upon a respectable young man at the late Widnes athletic sports. As proceedings of a civil char- actre- were also to be taken against the inspector in the County Court, he should be glad if the hearing of the case of assault could be allowed to stand over until the civil pro- ceeding had terminated, and it could not be commenced, according to the Act of Parliament, without giving Barnett a month's notice.—The Chairman intimated that the sum- mons had already been called on, and they could not re-open the matter that day.—The Inspector said he should press for the summons which be bad taken out against the client of Mr. Bartlett for disorderly conduct at the sports, being heard in the usual course.—We understand that the two cases will be contested very closely, and there is likely to be some very lively proceedings at the Widnes court next Wednesday. There are several witnesses on both sides. A GAME CASE—Thomas Weldron was charged with having trespassed on land at Farnworth, for the purpose of killing game. About half-past eleven on Monday evening, as P.C. Nicholson was on duty near the Horns public-house, Derby-road, he heard a dog bark in a certain field. He went to the place, and found the prisoner under the hedge. He took him into custody, and found upon him a gun in several pieces, a shot bag, and a powder flask. On charging the prisoner with having the gun in his possession for the pur- pose of killing game, he replied "It is no use telling a lie. I was on the field for the purpose of taking hares and rabbits" —ln reply to the Bench, the Inspector of Police stated that the prisoner had been 16 times previously convicted.—Pri- Roper was fiord 20s. and costs, and, in default, be imprisoned one month. The gun, powder flask, and shot bag were ordered to be sold for the benefit of the county.

THE MERSEY SALT AND BRINE COMPANY (LIMITED). The first ordinary general meeting of this company was held on Thursday, at Drapers'-gardens, Throgmorton-street, London. Mr. Cecil Raikes, who occupied the chair, said that as the shareholders would have perceived from the notice convening the meeting, it was only a formal one, called in accordance with the provisions of the Act of Par- liament regulating joint-stock companies. He and his col- leagues however, were very glad to be able to meet the shareholders, and to congratulate them upon the announce- ment made in the circular convening the meeting and the report which accompanied it. The following is the report alluded to, which was taken as read:— TO THE CHAIRMAN AND IRECTORS OF THE MERSEY SALT AND BRINE.COMPANY (LIMITED). GENTLEMEN,--It IS with much pleasure I sun now able to report to you , hat our boring for brine at Marbury, which has been going on for the last six weeks, proved yesterday to be extremely successful, when we came upon brine at a depth of 171 feet from the surface. On tapping the brine, it rose to the great height of 48 feet from the rock head, which is a proof of a very large supply. Toe company may now safely calculate upon having a supply of brine that will he considerably more than sufficient for the proposed requirements. I have had the brine carefully tested, and it proves to be of full strengn.h, one gallon (imperial) yielding albs. 20zs. of salt The boring has also proved that there will be a considerable saving effected in the pumping, as brine has been met with at a much lesser distance from the surface than the calculations were based upon.—l am, gentlemen, your obedient servant, EDWARD G. AMAN. Marbury, near Northwich, 12th July, 1881. The engineer of the company had been, accordingly, requested to prepare specifications for the works, which he hoped would be commenced next month or se. The only resolution which he would have to submit would be one as to the reappointment of Messrs. Qui'ter, Ball, and Co., as auditors of the company.—The Chairman, in reply to a shareholder, said that the supply of brine would be equal to the whole of the supply of tiles works at Runcorn. If any more should be required, by sinking a further shaft to the bottom of the rock there would be practically an un- limited supply of brine of the fullest strength—The resolu- tion reappointing the auditors was adopted, and a vote of thanks to the Chairman brought the proceedings to a close. laced

Sr. HELENS SHOP ASSISTANTS' ASSOCIATION. The usual meeting of the association was held on Tuesday, at the Market Tavern Cafe, Mr. CoHinson presiding. The reports of the distributors of hills for Bank Hulid ty closing were given in, showing that the holiday would be generally observed. It having been stated at a previous meeting that some of the principal drapers were desirous of closing their respective establishments at seven p.m., they were waited ! upon by Mr. J. Sharpies, who ascertained that Messrs. Marsh, Sharpies, Sutton, Porter and Co., and Cook, were willing to Close at seven p.m., independently of others every day but Saturday, cammimcing fr:m Tuesday, August 2nd. Several others were also willing, hot could not clearly see their rvay at present. It is hoped that the ladies of St. Helens will consider the assistants by making their purchases before seven p.m., and supporting' the early closing establish,nents, as, by doing so, the assos!iation feels that in a very short time every establishment y :d be closed at aeven p.m.

The ultimately agreed by the plaintiff that he would consent to grant, which bears date 10th December, 37, Henry VIII take the promise of defendant to faithfnlly pay him 3+. per (1545) conveys to Sir Richard the manor of Norton, the site per week during his lifetime, on condition that be made no and house of the old monastery with the high and lower further claim upon the goods.—The proceedings in the case court, the "fermery orchard," great garden, smith's orchard, then terminated. Enley Wood, several messuages and lands in Stockham. with all the rents from the preceding Lady Day. The price paid by Sir Richard Brooke for his purchase was £1,512 Is. 9d., and the yearly reserve rent of .£7 18s., which altogether was about equivalent to 22 years' purchase upon £7B 19s. Id., the sum stated to be the annual rent of the I property. Norton Priory, the seat of Sir Richard Brooke, occupies the sight of the canonry, and is an old quadrangular edifize (which was besieged in 1643), and stana in a park of about 115 acres. The present Sir Richard hAs taken great interest in the Priory, and has restored the I crypt since he enteral into possession. Though the house with its refectory, dormitory, and other offices has passed away and left no trace behind them, the few fragments of work in stone which still remain sufficiently attest the canons' skill as artificers and builders, and prove them to have been men of taste. The beautiful doorway and some very fine vaultings which go back to the first foundation of the house, and than which nothing finer could be executed now, are still preserved in the present house. The semi- circular arches of this doorway are enriched with elaborate foliage and other ornaments and rest upon pillars with sculptured capitals ; and the vaults originally consisted of groined arches springing from short octagonal columns with capitals. A second doorway corresponding with the original one just described has been erected by the present baronet. The floor of the cryp;. is covered with tiles ornamented with the Norton Arms, and the crypt itself is embellished with artistically carved old oak furniture in a high state of preservation. A chest at the end of the crypt hears the date of 1687 in very legible figures. Close by this I chest is an elaborately carved mantel piece, enriched with the coat of arms, and also a brass plate, on which are the following words : ~ ' "Though warmth the coming guest to cheer, Be kindled on the hearthstone here, Rill warmer when he mounts the stair. The welcome that awaits him there." Considerable interest was centred in a hat stand made of oak , and horns of deer, several helmets and breast plates, together with a number of bronze busts; while in various parts of the - • - were exhibited the skins and antlers of several wild pa 55,....,. animaia. Ascsnding the stairs the visitor's attention wad directed to an extensive oil painting upon the wall, the eat). Jed of which was illustrative of the mode of travelling in the tims of Charles IL, and the work of the present Sir Richard. On the first landing there was a large window splendidly illuminated with the Norton coat of arms, and a little further on was an antiquated clock bearing date 1663. o,her works of art from the hand of the present owner of the Priory, numerous antlers, the head of a fine Moose deer, from New Brunswick, killed by a nephew of Sir Richard, and other results of the chase, were shown. The present baronet discovered the burial ground of the old abbots and made a small cemetery, of which great care has been taken. In the garden there is an incised sepulchral slab and a few other sculptured fragments which were dug up before 1856, towards the north-west corner of the house. Very many of the religions houses in old time were in the habit of setting up some saint as their special protector. In most seaports Saint Nicholas, as the popular saint to whom sailors paid their I homage, had the preeminence' no less than 370 churches ' being dedicated to him in England. At Norton, however, which from its first foundation looked out upon a great and stormy river, St. Christopher, whom the ignorant believed to have the care of such a stream, was chosen as second patron of the house. The legend of St. Christopher, or the Christ bearer, was meant to allegorise the Christian's passage over the stormy waves of thie troublesome world, and at Norton, as elsewhere, the saint is represented AS of gigantic size, carrying a child he had brought over the stream near which he was said to live. The gigantic figure ' occupies a conspicuous position in front of the house. Many persons found pleasure in strolling through the well kept gardens, which were brilliant with floral adornment,and In visiting the greenhouses, which were replete with vines, exotic and other plants, and the well-stocked kitchen gardens. On approaching the greenhouses the nlfactive senses were gratified by a delightful fragrance imparted by a number of rose trees tat h bent under the weight of the beautiful speci- mens they bore. From she Priory was cibtained an excellent view of the ruins of Hilton Castle, which was built about the time of the Conquest,ttnd was the favourite hunt- ing seat of John of Gaunt and the ,Duchy of Lancaster. It • the time of th'ecivil war of Charles 1., was dismantled in in and now inclodes a habitable martion which was rebuilt is the time of the Restoration. From beside the ruins rose the spire of Halton Church, which is a chapel of ease of the parish of Runcorn, of which Sir Richard Brooke is the lay rector. In the evening the bands played for dancing, and flue opportunity of tripping it on the newly-mown green- sward of the Priory was largely embraced.

RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS. Mr. John Ashton presided at the fortnightly meeting held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday. Present :—The Rev. J. W N. Tanner, Messrs. Handley, Hazlehurst, Norman, Fisher, Highfield, Mithrood, Jackson, James Darbyshire, Mclntyre, H. Linaker (clerk), and W. EL Linaker ,(deputy clerk).

THE VISFI' TO CHESTER ASYLUM. The Rev.J. W. N. TANNER said the committee appointed by the Board visited Chester Lunatic Asylum on Wednes- day last. There were IS males and 13 females chargeable to the Union, at present inmates of the asylum, and they were being well cared for; but none were in a St state for removal. The kindness and courtesy of Dr. Davidson, the superintendent, was greatly appreciated. STATE OF THE HOUSE. The number of inmates in the house was 170, correspond- ing week last year. 157. There were 15 imbeciles in the house. Fifty-seven children—boys and girls—were attend- ing school, and 37 were receiving industrial training. Dur- ins,. the week 590 persons had been relieved at a cost of £59 12s. 3d., corresionding week List year 661 persons at a cost of £64 24. 3d.

RUNCORN POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before Messrs. R. M. Brooke (chairman) aP Wm. Banks. USING AN UNREGISTERED BOA T.—John Hulse, of Station- road, Winsford, was summoned for using an unregistered boat as a dwelling.—Mr. Farrington, inspector of canal boats to the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority, said that on the sth net.. he was in the township of Sutton, and met the boat Ann, which belongs to the defendant, on the Weaver canal. It was not registered, and the man who was in charge of it said he did not know how it was that the vessel was not, as he bad asked his master about it several times.—Defendant was fined 5s , and 13s. 6d. costs. THE OLD Woman's REVENGE.—An old woman named Martha Bennett was convicted of having committed damage to the amount of sixpence by knocking down a rail belong- ing to John Morris, on the 11th inst.— Defendant admitted the offence, but said she bad been provoked to knock the fence down as she believed he had killed three of her ducks. She was sorry for what she had done.—Defendant was fined 5s ,and ordered to pay 61 damage, arid 108. 6d. costs. USING PROFANE LANGUAGE IN CHURCH-STREET.—Emme Sadler, nee Bostock, who is well known to the police, was fined 20s. and costs 12s. 6,1., or, in default of payment, one month's imprisonment, for using profane language in Church-street, on the 17th inst.—Alice Rothwell, Church- street, was similarly charged, and was fined 20s. and costs 12s. 6d., or, in default of payment, one month's imprison- ment.—The money was paid in both cases. Evidence was I.S.ven by P.C.'s Baker and Clark. TUESDAY.—Before Messrs. John Brundrit, and Henry Reynolds.

THE LIVERPOOL COMMISSION AGENT WHO MISSED HIS TRAIN. Mr. John Siephens, a respectably dressed man, described as a Liverpool commission agent, was charged with being drunkand refusing to leave the Railway Hotel licensed premises. Mr. Wm. Green, the landlord of the public house, which is near the railway station, said that between ten and eleven o'clock on the previous night, the prisoner entered the house. He was in the kitchen, and heard prisoner using language which was not of a very choice description to the servant in the bar. He went there and told the prisoner, who was not quite sober, to go out, but he ref used.—Defendant said he missed his train at about half-past five, and he afterwards had a cup of tea and some drink," which overcame him. He was very sorry.—Defendant was ordered to pay a fine of 15s. and costs, ss. 4d., or, in default be sent to prison 14 days. A gentleman who was present offered himself as surety for the money, and Stephens was set at liberty. THLIRSDAY.—Before Mr. S. B. Chadwick. THE ASSAULT WITH A STONE WEIGHING 14u3s.—Thomas Conway (18), dock labourer, charged with maliciously wounding Thomas Giblin, also a labourer, by striking him on the forehead with a granite sett weighing 14lbs. The principal portion of the evidence was simply a repetition of the facts which have already appeared in The Examiner. The complainant was able to appear on this occasion.—Dr. McDougall said he first gait the prosecutor on the 19th inst., at his house in Back Mersey-street. He had some difficulty in rousing him even to a state of half conscious- ness. On the following day he again saw him, and he seemed to be recovering from the effects of what appeared to be concussion of the brain. He examined the man's forehead, and found a cut wound extending from the inner angle of the left eye, across the nose, to the middle of the right eyebrow. There was also another wound from the outer angle of the right eye, and extending across the cheek about an inch. He thought the wounds were such as might have been produced by the sharp end of the granite paving stone produced.—Sergeant McMichael stated that he appre- hended the prisoner, who, in reply to the charge, said he had nothing to say.—Conwav, in reply to Mr. Johnson, deputy magistrates' clerk, said 'he did not wish ,o make any state- ment, and he was committed to the Knutsford Quarter Sessions for trial.

div.head: INTERESTING SToRY OF A _SIKH
div.p: INTERESTING SToRY OF A _SIKH
INDIAN.

An intelligent looking and neatly dressed black, who gave I his name as Abdullah. appeared at the Warrington Borough i Court, on Wednesday, befare Alderman Davies and Coun- cillor Fairclough, to ask the Bench to assist him in returning to India. He could speak English moderately well, though with such volubility, that it was with difficulty his meaning could be grasped. His story was a most interesting one.l Seven years since, when he was 16 years of age, Abdullah was living in his father's house in Lahore, Punjaub, India better known as the Sikh country, distant from Calcutta 1,772 miles. His father and brother held various positions, one of them being an officer in the 15th Sikh Cavalry. At this time Captain Warren of the Royal Engineers asked Abdullah's father permission to allow the lad to accompany him through the north-western provinces in the capacity ef valet. His father assented, and Abdullah travelled thousands of miles with his master, whose duty it was to make sur- veys of the roads, rivers and natural fortifications for the late Government. During the Afghan war Captain Warren did good service attended in the most faithful manner by Abdullah. After leaving Candahar, Captain Warren was ordered to that part of China recently occupied by Russia, visiting on his journey a number of military stations in Bengal. From China he was ordered to the imalers of Persia, to survey, &a., thence back to India. Here the Cap- tain's wife died. Abdullah was then brought with the children to England, when Captain Warren was sent to Zululand. He left Abdullah with the children in England, and by whom they were attended with great care. Unfortunately the captain was killed by Zulus, being surprised in the long grass and assegaied. Abdullah did not know the date, but thought it was two days prior to the death of the Prince Imperial. Captain Warren's household was then broken up, and the children were sent to a Continental school. Since then Abdullah has drifted about, being assisted by military men who have been in India and know the bravery and hoepit rlity of the Sikh Indian. He had been able to obtain some Indian essential oils, from which he manufactured a pleasing scent. He was very abstemious, and could live on curry and rice in the summer and save money for his passage, if the English people would only buy from him.—Replying to Mr. White, he said the people would not bny the scent at 2s. a bottle, and he had given it away. It was two years since he camel to England, and Ito had been trying to get back to India but I could not. He had been in every ship in Liverpool, but could not get to work his passage.—Aldertnan Davies: You seem to have got out of the world. I don't see why you come to Warrington. You should go to Liverpool.—Mr. White : He has just come frotn there.—Mr. Davies: It is a great mistake to come to England.—The Bench ultimately granted him 2s. 6d. with which to go to Liverpool.— Abdullah: Me none go to Liverpool; no, no. Me want go , to Lahore.—Alderman Davies: If we give you half a crown you can go to Jericho if you like.—The applicant then left the court.

BAPTIST SUNDAY SCHOOL, EARLESTOWN.—The anniver- sary services of this school were held On Sunday last, in the Co-operative Hall, Earle-street, when eloquent sermons were preached by the Rev. H. Hall, in the morning and evening. Notwithstanding the unfavourable weather, there was a good attendance. Mr. Hall delivered an address to parents and children in the afternoon. At each service ap- propriate liyines were sune, by the children. The collections realised £l3 14s. SUDDEN DEATH AT NEWTON.—Agnes Howard, the wife of John Howard, of Ashton-road, Newton, died suddenly on Tuesday morning. On Monday night deceased went to bed apparently in her usual health. In the middle of the night, however, she complained of being unwell, and her husband gave her a little whiskey. About three o'clock on Tuesday morning, she became much worse. A doctor was sent for, hut before he could arrive she expired. The cause of death is believed to have been heart disease EARLESTOWN WESLEYAN CHAPEL.—Two sermons weie preached in this place of worship on Sunday, by the Rev. J. C. Stanfield, and the Rev. A. Taylor. The services were well attended, and collections made on behalf of the Liver • pool Conference expenses realised .£4. VULCAN WESLEYAN CHAPEL, EARLE,TOWN.—The anni- versary services of this chapel were held on Sunday last. The preachers were the Revs. J. Bell and S. Pascal. There was a good attendance and collections were made at each service on behalf of the school funds. FUNERAL OF M R.J. H. EVANS.—The funeral of Mr. Josiah Hadfield Evans, of the firm of at s,rs. R. E. Evans and Co., Haydock Collieries, who met his death whilst bathing on one of the fiords in Norway, took place at the Congrega- tional Church, Newton-le-Willows, on Thursday. Ihe Rev. James Hallett, assisted by the Rev. Edwin Simon, Manchester, performed the funeral service. Among those who followed deceased Bs the grave were Mrs. Evans, Miss Lily Evans, and Mr, A. Evans (mother, sister, and brother of deceased) ; Messrs. Samuel and George Hadfield, of Manchester (uncles of the deceased); Mr. Richard Puking- ton, Rainford Hall ; Mr. Aifiad l'ilkington, Eccles ; Mr. Wm. Evans, Huvton ; Messrs. Drayton Grimke, and John N. Marsden. A large number of miners employed at the collieries and scholars from the Haydock schools followed in procession. The body was enelos-d in a metallic shell, and covered with a polished oak coffin. Deceased was only 23 years of age. •

MAKINSON AND WILCOCK, in returning their sincere thanks to their numerous patrons and the public generally for the very kind and liberal support they have hitherto received, hope, by striet attention to the interests of their clients, and the prompt and faithful discharge of their duties, to continue to merit the same; the more so, as they are able to offer ad- vantages not generally enjoyed by those engaged in the same business, Mr. Makinson having had from early youth practical experience f the English Timber, Stone and Building Trades, and of Farming in all its branches, being at the present time a farmer himself on a large scale; and, in addition, having served his apprenticeship to the ENGINEERING and MILLWRIGHT busi- ness. besides having had, during the last TEN years, consider- able practice 1,, Valuing and Selling Coliery, Quarry, and other Machinery and Working Plant, Growing nd Fallen Timber, Farming Stocks, Growing and Gathered Produce, Stocks-in- Trade, Household Furniture Innkeepers' Effects, Houses, Buildings, Landed Estates and Property generally, and also in cases involving Damage and Trespass. Mr. WILCOCK, also, has had the advantage of being brought up to Farming, together with that of having served an appren- ticeship to an eminent Veterinary Surgeon, combined with the experience he has had since his connection with this firm, enables him to give judicious and valuable advice in all eases in which he may be consulted. In conclusion, M. and W. beg their friends and the public generally to note that they have a trustworthy and efficient staff of assistants in their employ, who have been carefully trained to watch over the interests of those who favour the firm with their patronage; whilst last, but not least, their system of advertising, and the facilities they possess Of ensuring an extensive circulation, enable them to offer the utmost pos- sible) üblicitv to any sales entrusted to their management.
